en: Preface to the Record of Myriad Dharmas Returning to the Mind:
I am not a follower of the Śākya clan, yet I take pleasure in the scriptures of the Śākyas. It is not that I favor the Śākyas;

rather, I favor the Śākyas because they are identical to the teachings of the Master Kǒng. The books of the Master Kǒng are level, accessible, and grounded in reality; both the wise and the ignorant follow them. The [scriptures] of the Śākyas...

This book is subtle, wondrous, profound, and deep; it is difficult to explain at every door. If, within that which is subtle, wondrous, profound, and deep, one can nevertheless remain level, accessible, earnest, and substantial, then it may be said that the teachings of Śākyamuni are comparable to the books of Confucius.
The *Record of the Ten Thousand Dharmas Returning to the Mind* was composed by Master Zu-yuan of Xiao Yangshan.
The Master’s spiritual integrity was transcendent and profound; he directly penetrated the Unsurpassed [Buddhahood] and took pity on...

The sea of suffering is vast and boundless. Desiring to lift this entire world and cause it all to reach the other shore, I have therefore composed this record to awaken the multitude from their delusions.
Why is its title "The Ten Thousand Dharmas Return to the Mind"? It is because the mind is fundamentally ultimate emptiness; it envelops all existence.

When released, it flows through the six directions of the universe; when turned back, it does not fill a single handful. This is what Zhouzi called "the Ultimateless (Wuji) giving rise to the Great Ultimate (Taiji)," and what the *Zhongyong* [describes as]...

This refers to the Great Root and the Thorough Way—the "One Thread" (*yìguàn*) spoken of by the Master [Confucius], and the "washing of the mind and withdrawing into secrecy" (*xǐxīn tuìcáng yú mì*) mentioned in the *I Ching*.
All of these are found herein. Now, let us examine this record one by one: in the questions concerning worldly matters, we see how good and evil are distinguished according to Confucianism;
in the questions concerning Confucianism and Buddhism, we see how they are identical in their Way (*dào*); and in the questions concerning Buddhism...

This distinguishes him from the ordinary monastic community. When he expounded upon the principles of Chan to realize Bodhi, it was as clear and radiant as the sun and stars traversing the heavens—truly a sight to behold.

While many Chan masters of the past have left behind recorded sayings (*yulu*) whose subtle words and wondrous insights are not easily understood, this record alone is profoundly penetrating and illuminating; it is utterly frank and straightforward, yet also exceedingly profound and refined.
It is profoundly profound and sublime, yet also utterly plain and practical. Those of superior capacity who hear it may perceive their nature and clarify their minds;

those of inferior capacity who hear it will likewise find it sufficient for cultivating the self and sparing themselves from transgression. Although it shares the same status as the books of the Four Sages, being chanted within every home and household—how could this not be possible?
I have heard that in the West, the Supreme Vehicle does not establish itself in language or written words; is this record not, then, merely the "Fenggan" (the Talking Tree) of that tradition?
Are you being prolix? However, that which does not rely on language or writing is for the purpose of clarifying the fundamental principle (zong);
language and writing are for the purpose of expanding the teaching (jiao). Since the principle and the teaching are from the outset not two, then speech is identical to silence.
Only when one knows that speech is identical to silence may one be permitted to read this record.

I considered that in our Confucian tradition, the succession of the thousand sages has held that there is no dharma outside the mind; since all dharmas arise from the mind, by grasping the one, the myriad can be unified, and by combining the myriad, one does not depart from the one.
Apart from this principle, things cannot help but become discordant. Now, upon examining the recorded sayings of Master Zuoyuan, [he] takes the myriad...
The Dharma takes the mind as its fundamental principle; how remarkably this accords with the tenets of our Confucian tradition!

As for those who are said to be like water cascading from a high eaves or a rushing torrent—possessing unimpeded eloquence—how could a fool like me fathom their depths? Yet, when one examines the true and definitive meaning [of their teaching], it is found to be in perfect harmony.

Lamp after lamp continues in succession; as it is, it remains indestructible. It possesses its own solar radiance, giving rise to the currents of the vast ocean and shaking Mount Kunlun, yet it does not manifest any phenomenal form.
Having attained great sovereign mastery, it does not depend on grasping the light in a mirror or scooping up water from a ladle to perceive it through faint and blurred semblances.
Indeed, regarding the Buddha-dharma from the time of Mazu until before Dahui, the direct mandate for engaging with sentient beings was entirely...
This reveals the great capacity and great function [of the teaching]. Thereafter, though there were thousands of branches and ten thousand streams, they all converged back into a single source.

Just as among teachers, friends, and brothers, they mutually assist one another for edification and benefit—what appears as contention in worldly affairs is, in the Buddha-dharma, a harmonious exchange of verses.
Those who have submitted themselves to this teaching can understand the intent of this record; it can be drawn upon from the immediate and inferred from the distant. It can...
Speaking in terms of "explaining" (shi), one may explain; yet even without speaking of explaining, there is nothing that is not explaining.

This lies within the capacity of those who are vessels for the Mahāyāna, and they cannot transcend its boundaries; how much less could those of shallow learning and beginners dare to look at the precipice and think of retreating?

As for illumination and function, provisional and ultimate, their discernment and mutual interplay, and the clear sequence of host and guest, do not depend on verbal expression—how could they possibly require it?

A former scholar once said: "It is the same principle. When Confucians grasp it, they become Confucians;
when Buddhists grasp it, they become Buddhists; when immortals grasp it, they become immortals. Although their aims differ in their paths, the principle is fundamentally one and the same.

Therefore, when Master Wang Yangming spoke of Confucianism with others, he constantly used the tenets of the Buddhist school to elucidate it; when he spoke of Chan with monks, he constantly used Confucian texts to instruct them.
This does not merely demonstrate his skill in observing Confucianism; it also demonstrates his skill in elucidating Buddhism.

Now, as for what is called "Buddhism," it is not the case that one has fully entered the mountain gates, sat in a quiet chamber, struck the fish-shaped gong, and warmed oneself with incantations before one can be said to have transcended the realm of mundane dust.

It is intended to eliminate delusive thoughts and return to True Suchness (*tathatā*). While worldly people transform wisdom (*jñāna*) into consciousness (*vijñāna*), the Tathāgata desires that people transform consciousness into wisdom.
While worldly people obscure their inherent nature (*prakṛti*) to indulge their passions, the Tathāgata desires that people draw those passions back to return to their nature.
In this regard, it truly accords with the Confucian intention of restraining desire and preserving principle. From the perspective of one's own mind—

Heedfulness consists in observing the precepts, maintaining vigilance, and being cautious when alone. When one’s own mind is free from the notions of self and other, that constitutes the equality of all dharmas.
To insist on distinguishing this from Confucianism as two separate systems is an error. The *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
“The Tathāgata has taught nothing at all. The *Śūraṅgama Samādhi Sūtra* states: “All verbal explanations are devoid of real meaning; they are the pure Dharma. Thus, it is the pure Dharma.
The Essence: It does not rely on verbal expression and does not fall within the realm of spoken truth. This is indeed the secret instruction of the Supreme Vehicle;

yet, what need is there for the various texts of the Great Canon? Nevertheless, those of superior intelligence realize it by turning the mind back upon itself, while those of middling capacity contemplate its meaning upon opening a volume.
Thus, what are called "lettered Prajñā" and "contemplation of the true mark" stand side-by-side with [direct realization] as the three [forms of Prajñā]. This is the position of the Chan school.
This refers to using the "secret mouth" in place of the bitter gourd to lead people into the profound.

Master Zuyuan compiled a record titled *The Ten Thousand Dharmas Return to the Mind*. Now, as for the mind, it is the essence of true suchness (*tathatā*); as for dharmas, they are the function of true suchness.
The mind cannot exist apart from dharmas as its source, nor can dharmas exist apart from the mind as their governing principle. Thus, the *Vajra*...
The Sūtra states: "The Tathāgata is the meaning of the suchness of all dharmas; that is to say, suchness is immovable, and there is constant, clear knowing.
This Chan Master was a renowned elder among the people of the capital, having received the authentic transmission of Linji.
He compiled a work that examined the learning of Li Ao and Zhu Xi (Kao-xing) to elucidate the unsurpassed school of Bodhi. May it be called the *Xing Shi* (Exposition on Practice). It is as follows:

It may be called "aiding the Confucian. Yet those who are wise in this world seek the beginning beyond words through words, and contemplate the source of written expression through that which is wordless.
Thus, they do not transcend the two characters "quiescence" and "illumination," wherein mountains, rivers, and the great earth fully reveal the Dharma-body;
and where earth, water, fire, and wind all lack substantial reality, while the world’s infinitesimal...

Since neither the phenomena of the mundane world nor their symbolic representations are sufficient to bind his mind, he will not be obstructed by the meaning of the Prajñā of Words and Characters, and he will not fail the intention of Master Zuyuan Chan in compiling this collection; it is hoped that he may thereby attain realization.

Preface.
The mind is the substance of all phenomena; all phenomena are the function of the mind. Phenomena do not depart from the mind; they are like waves being water.

The substance can give rise to function, just as water moving forms waves. Thus, one knows that all phenomena are nothing but the mind. The mind is fundamentally empty and quiescent; names are established for it because of phenomena.
Pure phenomena consist of humans, devas, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas. Defiled phenomena consist of asuras.
The realms of animals, hells, and hungry ghosts, though differing in their defilement or purity, are all but shadows of the mind.
If one awakens to the fact that the true mind is fundamentally empty, the myriad dharmas will naturally vanish away.

Now, Chan Master Zuyuan of Xiaoyang Mountain is the grandson of the Elder Fushí of Tunchen and the son of Venerable Tianfeng of Shanglan in Jiangxi. He has thoroughly investigated the scriptural teachings and attained profound mastery.
The Chan School has realized the primary meaning and attained the supreme vehicle; its eloquence is unimpeded, for it is truly the banner of the Dharma.
Out of compassion, the Chan Master guides and exhorts later students by presenting this *Guixin Lu* (Record of Returning to the Mind), which directly points to the wondrous source.

Within this *Jishi Lu* (Record of the Ultimate Reality), every word reveals one's nature and every sentence clarifies the mind; it is capable of washing away perverse attachments and sweeping away heterodox views, leading directly to realization.
Bodhi! To attain Buddhahood all at once—this is truly a compassionate vessel for the sea of suffering and a virtuous guide on the diverging paths.

In my past lives, I have been fortunate enough to encounter this text; my doubts are instantly severed, and the ground of my mind is made clear. As for myself, my talent is clumsy and my learning meager.
Knowing that my insight and vision are shallow, I am insufficient to elucidate the profound and abstruse; I have merely composed this brief preface to manifest the kindness of my teacher.

Preface by Liu Fang, a retired scholar of the ancient Yan state, who has washed his hands with reverence:

The Record of All Dharmas Returning to the Mind narrates its own origins from before the void kalpa, beyond the limit of majestic sound (*bhīṣmagarjita*). At that time, neither Buddhas nor sentient beings had names; each possessed a single, perfectly luminous mirror.
Because sentient beings are without [intrinsic] reality, within the pure white light, they momentarily give rise to a stirring mind that obscures their original luminosity.

This transforms into the worlds and the karmic fruits of sentient beings; birth and death follow one another in an unceasing succession. They remain mired in the three realms, crawling through the nine states of existence.
From delusion until now, there has been no day of awakening. If you do not sever the current and return to the source, when will you finally be able to achieve sudden liberation?
You must realize that the myriad dharmas all return to the one mind, thereby transforming worldly wisdom into Buddha-wisdom.

This may be likened to uniting the hundred rivers into a single moisture, compressing the multitude of dust motes into a single pellet, melting bracelets and bangles into a single piece of gold, or transforming butter and curd into [a single essence].
This single flavor is the Dharma of the One Mind, wherein principle and phenomena are perfectly complete. All Buddhas of the ten directions and all sentient beings are identical to this mind;

it lacks nothing and has no excess. While the Buddhas have already awakened to it, sentient beings remain unaware. Thus, there arise the designations of "ordinary" and "sage," or "delusion" and "enlightenment.
The ignorant are unwilling to fold their hands and look on from the sidelines; therefore, I point out this one true path for returning to the mind. As the ancients said: "The Wondrous High Mountain."
At the summit, from the very beginning, deliberation was not permitted. On the second peak, the various patriarchs allowed for a degree of discussion and understanding;

thus, they provisionally formulated questions and answers to explain ten categories of names and characteristics, thereby verifying the single mind and universally bestowing its benefits upon all sentient beings.

First, to awaken those deluded by worldly ways and cause them to turn away from evil and return to goodness. Second, to discuss principles with Confucians and sweep away heterodox slanders. Third, to [accord with] the Way...

1. Discerning the False: Do not seek outside. 2. Sudden Enlightenment and Cultivation-Realization: Directly transcending to the realm of the Buddhas. 3. The Distinctions of the Teachings and Vehicles:
Subtly demonstrating the single mind. 4. Pure Land as Mind-Only: The Buddha does not come from without. 5. The Five Schools of Chan:
Their principles are of one essence. 6. The Ten Demons Disturbing the Right: Nurturing the Way through prevention. 7. Scriptural Explanations.
Citing evidence to sever doubts and inspire trust. Tenth, exhorting others toward goodness by printing and distributing [this work] as a way to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Attached hereto are twenty verses of detached couplets from my mountain retreat. With the meager roots of goodness planted in my youth, I have happened to catch a glimpse of the Ultimate Way;

thus, I venture to extend my narrow perspective, requesting correction from the Great Vehicle. This is truly not based on my own conjectures, but follows solely the Buddha-vehicle. Should there be future descendants who read this record...
I beg your compassion and repent for the transgression of misrepresenting the Dharma. If this accords with the Sage’s heart, I shall follow the teachings and practice accordingly.
May we meet together in the future at the Dragon Flower Assembly, where we shall have the fortune to receive the prediction of our attainment of Buddhahood.

A worldly person, seeking to awaken from delusion, asked me: "I wish to remain constantly in plain simplicity; would there be any merit in this? The Master said: "The scales and shells of fish and turtles, and the feathers and wings of birds—though the bodies of these various classes differ, their capacity for perception and sensation of pain and itching is no different from that of humans.
It is all because of erroneous thoughts during one's previous life that the physical forms of this present world have come to be."

This is different. If one truly maintains sincerity and faith, abstaining from meat and observing the precept against killing, such a person is truly a virtuous gentleman and may be called a benevolent and compassionate man.
If one thus observes the fasts and precepts throughout their life without weariness, not only will their merit, fortune, and longevity increase, but they will also plant the true cause for Bodhi.

Alas, how lamentable it is that the world is deluded and lacks wisdom; people greedily crave flavors and indulge their bellies in slaughter, committing hundreds of kinds of deeds while regarding themselves as noble.

With this three-inch tongue, one day you will change heads and faces, transmigrating through cycles of devouring and being devoured; at that time, your suffering, resentment, and regret will be such that no one can relieve them.
As the worldly saying goes:
"The people of the world all say that pigs, sheep, chickens, geese, scaly creatures, feathered birds, and so forth—these various beasts and fowl—are born by Heaven."

"This object serves as a vegetable for humans. If it were not slaughtered for food, what use would it be left for others? The Master said, "The people of this world consider eating meat to be entirely natural;
they slaughter at will, seeking to please their mouths and gratify their bellies.

They do not realize that all sentient beings of the water, land, and air are merely the retribution of their own karma, each receiving a physical form. Although the people of this world rely on [their senses] for a moment..."

...this merit. To deceive and kill others to fatten oneself—what resentment can there be against those whose strength is inferior and difficult to oppose? The day for settling such grievances will surely come.

If it is indeed the case that animals such as pigs and sheep were created by Heaven to serve as food for humans, then the jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice, as well as the countless other evil beasts and predatory birds in this world that are all capable of devouring humans—were these not likewise created by Heaven? Even if men and women were [created for the same purpose]...

"Is it permissible to use foul things as vegetables? The people of this world do not understand that the karma of killing must be repaid; instead, they groundlessly give rise to feelings of resentment.
This is the height of ignorance. A common saying goes:
'I have often heard people say that their hearts are more intent on being superior than observing the vegetarian fast. What is the reasoning behind this? The Master said:
A benevolent and virtuous gentleman, a compassionate and good person, benefits sentient beings and rescues all things, accumulating merit and building up virtue.

Even amidst the sphere of daily activities and wherever they act spontaneously, upon seeing any living being cast into the realm of death, they cannot fail to feel compassion and rescue them back to the land of life.
Only such compassion can be called a "good heart. To kill another without cause in order to satisfy oneself is not so.

For the sake of their mouths and bellies, some hold sharp knives to slit open the belly, while others grasp pointed blades to pierce the heart; they flay the skin and scrape off the scales, severing throats and splitting shells.

They boil them alive and fry them raw, stewing them in cauldrons and roasting them over furnaces. Through hundreds of such tortures, they seek to satisfy their palates and gratify their stomachs, utterly devoid of any heart of compassion.
Where, then, lies their so-called "good heart"? Instead, they utter words that betray their conscience—how grave is their transgression!
I can offer repentance. My words are bitter now out of my foolishness, but you must listen attentively.

If you truly refrain from killing for the rest of your life and maintain a vegetarian diet without backsliding, even if your mind is not yet perfected and you fall among the common folk, you will at least avoid the hands of the butcher and the cauldrons and furnaces of hell.
The common saying goes: "Though I am poor and pure, I do not commit theft. The Master said: "To steal property is not the only way to be a thief.

Corrupting the virtuous, practicing deceitful arts and fraud, instigating litigation, luring others into prostitution or gambling, and ensnaring people in the criminal courts—these too are acts of thievery."

Those who force others into distress, harm others in perilous situations, bring others to danger, deplete others' wealth and goods, exchange others' fine things for inferior ones, fail to repay debts, encroach upon the ignorant, and rob the weak—all such unwholesome persons are thieves. If one possesses wisdom, [one should recognize this].

When seeing others who are wealthy and noble, one should give rise to a heart of longing and admiration, regretting that one did not cultivate merit in previous lives. One should recognize that the poverty and suffering experienced in this life are what must be personally endured as the result of past karma.
Thereupon, one should once again arouse faith, cultivating merit and accumulating virtue, refraining from all evils and wholeheartedly practicing all forms of goodness.
"By nature, one does not bring suffering upon those who have performed meritorious deeds and practiced goodness.
As the worldly saying goes: 'Take wealth with fairness; do not pursue greed or hoarding; seek it according to your lot. If one acts in this way, what could possibly go wrong? The Master said:
Wealth and goods should be acquired with fairness and propriety. Though they are called worldly treasures, accumulation over time becomes a source of calamity.

Do not amass what comes to you; do not let what is amassed endure for long. If one seeks through greed without satiety, or takes by force without shame, though one may attain wealth for a time, one cannot escape the dark subtraction from one’s bright ledger.
As the Buddhist sutras state: "The property of a person in their present life belongs to five families."
What are these five families? First, kings and government officials; second, water and fire; third, thieves and bandits;
fourth, weapons of war; and fifth, unworthy descendants. The foolish people of the world toil their entire lives, accumulating vast amounts of wealth in the hope of enduring prosperity.
Yet they do not realize that these five families have a claim upon it; in the end, it cannot avoid being dissipated. Thus it is.
"Even wealth acquired through fair means will not endure for long; how much less so that which is seized by force or obtained through fraud and deception—how could such things last forever?
As the worldly proverb says: 'I have always been of few desires and maintain only one wife; as for the act of sexual misconduct, I shall never, under any circumstances, commit it. The Master said:"
The two characters for "lust" (*kāma*) are the root of birth and death. Sexual misconduct and private adultery are the foremost of all evils;
they destroy the Way and ruin virtue, bringing calamity and leading to one's own destruction. From antiquity to the present day, these matters are difficult to describe in full.

Even cravings such as for wine or wealth can still be restrained with relative ease, yet this single barrier of lust is even more cruel and fierce. Why is this so? It is entirely because sentient beings...

One's nature and destiny are fundamentally governed by lustful desire, which perpetuates the cycle of birth and death. When past habits have become so deeply ingrained, how can the karma of desire be brought to an end without the illumination of wisdom?
It is difficult to sever these bonds while living at home; one must require that one's physical appearance be upright. If it is not one's own wife, one must certainly not engage in such acts.
There are certain vulgar fellows who, upon seeing a woman with even a slight degree of beauty, immediately give rise to depraved thoughts; they dwell upon her, long for her, covet her, and seek her.

Their heavenly principle is already obscured and their human heart is already lost. A Buddhist sutra says: "One who commits adultery with another's wife shall receive the retribution of having his lineage cut off;
one who commits adultery with another's unmarried daughter shall receive the retribution of having his descendants become lewd and dissolute. You may observe this generally; do not indulge in lust.
In households where depravity prevails, the source and flow of corruption follow this pattern of decline, often coming to the ears and eyes of the public. As the ancients said:

"I do not violate another's wife; others shall not violate my spouse. Furthermore, there is a class of sentient beings with deluded karma who, upon seeing the wives of others—who are fundamentally no different from their own—deem them beautiful and devise schemes to seduce and deceive them. There are even those who abandon their own wives without a second thought to consort with such debauched women.
There are those who, while still children, engage in illicit affairs with the wives of servants or subordinates, as well as various other acts of lust that cannot be fully enumerated.

Furthermore, there are literary men of talent who, praised for their momentary brilliance, describe the private passions of women within the inner chambers, compiling these into songs and ballads and publishing them as books.
They delude people into believing these accounts to be true, inciting depraved thoughts; their evil is as vast as a mountain. There is no end to it.
This is what one can pray for. If there are men or women possessed of wisdom, they must feel shame and repentance within themselves, and immediately sever the practice of sexual misconduct;
then they shall have a share in the realms of humans and devas. It is not that I am being bitter-mouthed in urging you; it is simply because the karma of sexual misconduct is so extremely evil.

The worldly saying goes: "If sexual misconduct is as evil as this, how much more so are the karmas of speech? The Master said: "Among the ten non-virtuous actions, there are four that pertain solely to speech:
false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech. To kill a person without shedding blood is an exceedingly grave transgression; it destroys the goodness of others."

To speak of others' shortcomings, to debate others' faults, to discuss others' transgressions, to deceive others of their wealth, and to hoodwink others of their possessions—even leading to the ruin of the Way and virtue, and the loss of both others and oneself—all stem from unrestrained speech; thus, one incurs manifold calamities.
The Sūtra says: The Buddha told Ānanda, "When human beings are born into this world, calamity issues from the mouth; one must guard the mouth more carefully than a fierce fire.
A fierce fire blazes up and burns away worldly wealth, but malicious speech blazes up and burns away the wealth of the seven treasures.
For all sentient beings, calamity issues from the mouth; it is the axe that carves the body and the disaster that destroys the person. Now, there are those who possess hidden virtue."
One must conceal evil and proclaim goodness; one’s speech must be truthful and one’s discourse free from falsehood. When questioned, one should respond with concise words and a gentle countenance.
Naturally, the Buddhas and devas will protect such a person, and the people of the world will love and revere them.

The common saying goes: "The foolish by nature love to drink; what can be done about it? The Master said: "Delusion of mind and loss of will, the ruin of families and the destruction of persons—these mostly arise from wine.
The calamities it brings are manifold. When people of the world indulge in drinking without satiety, they eventually come to the point where their very physical forms are disfigured and injured."

They pervert the rites of propriety, lie in the streets and revile the public thoroughfares, commit acts of insubordination that ruin their reputations, and engage in licentiousness that destroys their virtue.
Among such transgressions and rebellious acts, the craving for drink is the most extreme. As the ancients said: "I warn you not to honor drinking; it is a drug of madness, not a fine flavor.

It can transform a cautious and virtuous nature into that of a cruel and obstinate person. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that there are thirty-six kinds of faults associated with drinking alcohol. Not...
However, when people of the world drink alcohol, they fall into error; even Arhats, through their craving for drink, lose their supernormal powers.
How much more then should those who are beginners, ordinary beings, and sentient creatures still lost in delusion refrain from it and treat it with dread!
The worldly saying goes: "Please explain the thirty-six kinds of faults. The Master said: "The thirty-six kinds of faults of drinking alcohol are:
being unfilial toward one's parents; treating teachers and elders with contempt; failing to revere the Triple Gem; lacking faith in the sutras and the Dharma; and slandering śramaṇas."
They expose the faults of others, constantly speak falsehoods, falsely accuse others of evil deeds, engage in divisive speech by repeating rumors, and use harsh words that wound others.
These are the roots of illness and the foundation of strife; they cause an evil reputation to spread, making them loathed and detested by others, and lead them to reject the sages and worthies.

They bring resentment upon Heaven and Earth. They cause their undertakings to fall into ruin and their family wealth to be dissipated. They are constantly devoid of shame and lack any sense of modesty.

Without cause, they beat their slaves; they recklessly kill living beings; they commit adultery with the wives of others; they steal people's property; and they distance themselves from virtuous persons.

Associating with evil friends, they constantly harbor anger and resentment; day and night they are consumed by sorrow and anxiety. They are pulled eastward and dragged westward, held to the south and fastened to the north.

They fall into ditches or lie prostrate on the road; they tumble from carts or fall from horses; they encounter rivers and drown; they hold lamps and set them on fire; in the heat of summer, they perish from the scorching sun.
"In freezing cold, one dies of frostbite. Such are the faults of those who drink alcohol. A gentleman who cultivates virtue must personally guard against them.

As the worldly saying goes: "If someone has a fault, one should not become angry when insulted; even if there is a slight resentment, one should settle it with a single act of forbearance. The Master said:

Anger is the root of ten thousand obstacles; forbearance is the foremost of a hundred blessings. When people of the world speak of forbearance, they find the character for "forbearance" (ren) most difficult to practice.
Without great wisdom, one cannot achieve it resolutely. This is true except for Buddhas and patriarchs who remain unmoving in suchness; as for those who are beginners:
Many men of talent and heroism have met their downfall through this, falling into ignoble states. The Buddhist sutras state that patience is supreme.
There is a worldly proverb which says: "Only after one has been able to swallow three pecks of pungent vinegar can one truly become a prime minister.
If even ordinary people living in the world must act thus, how much more so for those who study the Way? How could they not be broad-minded and patient?
The common saying goes: "People of the world are mostly greedy; they amass vast wealth and property, wondering whether their descendants will later attain great fortune.
The Master said: "The foolish people of this world rely on power and influence, darken their hearts, and lose their virtue.

They employ every kind of clever trickery to seize wealth, yet even if they achieve sudden riches, how can they last? A man of wisdom must instead accumulate merit and cultivate virtue according to his lot."
Seeking through worldly means, one must simply follow the mandate of Heaven; thus, divine protection will naturally accrue, and blessings and prosperity will increase in secret.
Worldly people know they seek wealth for their descendants, yet they do not realize they should cultivate goodness and merit for them. What is meant by "cultivating merit"?

It is to revere the Triple Gem, accumulate hidden virtue, maintain strict family regulations, and instruct in agriculture and study—this is what it means to cultivate merit. What is meant by "seeking wealth"? It is to be insincere and lacking in integrity... [the text is incomplete].
To employ mental artifice and amass ill-gotten gains—this is how one seeks wealth. Those who seek wealth do not flourish; those who cultivate merit become manifest later.

Have you not seen that among the world’s great wealthy families, there are descendants who are unworthy, indulging as they please in prostitution and gambling, until in a single day they ruin the family estate and even lose their own lives?
Such cases occur frequently. Why do you not exercise wise discernment? As the proverb says: "What is gained comes obscurely; what is lost..."
"This is quite right. When a person of wisdom observes this, they cannot help but feel a chill in their heart.
As the worldly saying goes: "To regard everything as empty as taught above, yet to constantly examine oneself and strive to be a good person. The Master said:
To become a good person, one must examine oneself. Throughout the course of a single day, from morning until evening, one should reflect upon one's own mind and scrutinize one's own principles.

When every movement of thought and every stirring of intention accords with the Way of Heaven, and when all actions performed spontaneously accord with the affairs of humanity, one remains constantly alert and aware, never allowing private desires to leak forth.
After a long time, the mind becomes upright and human desires naturally empty away. It is like this.
They are negligent, indulging their passions and following their whims. They do not fear the punishments of heaven nor dread the retribution of their deeds.

Acting contrary to propriety and performing what is improper, they accumulate such heavy evil over the passage of days and months that, once their merit is exhausted, their various karmas confront them. While alive, they manifest calamities;
after death, they fall into the three miserable realms. As the Buddhist sutras say: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten. By reason of this...

"When the conditions converge and the time arrives, one must personally undergo the retribution of the fruit. Thus we know that cause and effect are never obscured; future generations must therefore maintain sincerity and faith.
A worldly saying goes: "Regarding the matter of cause and effect, many people do not believe. The Master said: "Cause and effect are never obscured; there is retribution."
There is no discrepancy; it is like a shadow following a form, without the slightest error. The former sages have explained this in great detail, yet later ignorant people do not believe it.
One must carefully observe all people of the world: there are those who are wealthy and noble, and those who are poor and lowly;

those whose lives are cut short, and those who live long; those who enjoy honor and favor, and those who suffer distress and disgrace; those who endure hardship, and those who dwell in peace and leisure; and those who attain the imperial examinations while still young.

There are those who live their entire lives without passing the imperial examinations; there are those with wealth and grain but no children; there are those facing hardship yet having many descendants;
there are those for whom suffering and joy are unequal across the beginning, middle, and end of life; and there are those who experience poverty or wealth throughout their whole lives until death.

Such variations are manifold, all resulting from the retribution of karma. As an ancient sage said: "Plant a single grain of millet in spring, and reap ten thousand seeds in autumn. Thus it is for human beings to cultivate goodness.

Evil. Its retribution is likewise such. Thus one knows that the suffering and joy of the three realms, and the ascent and descent within the six paths of existence, are all created by oneself and experienced by oneself;
they do not come from being bestowed by an external source.
The common saying goes: "I have seen families who are loyal, upright, and virtuous yet possess no grain to carry on their backs;

yet there are those who are sly, obstinate, and wicked who own ten thousand acres of fertile fields. Is the doctrine of cause and effect not mistaken? The Master said: "Goodness and evil are not equal."

The retributions of karmic fruit are not uniform. Some are repaid upon one's own person; some are repaid upon one's descendants; some are repaid in the present life; and some are repaid in future lives. There are those who eat coarse gruel and those who enjoy jade delicacies;

those clad in brocade robes and those in robes of tattered quail feathers. Furthermore, there are those who dwell in humble huts and those in golden palaces; those who possess a thousand horses and those who have but a single ladle.
All of this is the retribution for the good and evil one has personally committed during previous lives; the present experiences of suffering and joy are not subject to the slightest error or excess.

When one sees a cruel and wicked person enjoying wealth, how can one know that they cultivated merit in a prior life? Or when one encounters a benevolent and charitable person who is poor and dies young, it is due to the karmic bonds they formed in the past.
As Zhuangzi said: "The bandit Zhi had nine thousand followers and roamed across the world, plundering and oppressing the feudal lords, yet..."
Regarding longevity, the *Lunyu Shu* (Commentary on the Analects) states: "Xiang Mo was seven years old when he became the teacher of Confucius, yet he died young.

Thus, there are those who are upright and pure yet live in poverty, while others are corrupt and greedy yet possess great wealth. One must not, because of such discrepancies in the present life, cling to them and slander the prior causes as being erroneous."
The common saying goes: "The retribution for good and evil is unfailing in its principle. Yet there are certain fools who do not believe in cause and effect;
they even claim that the benevolent heart cannot produce rice, but if it could enter a cauldron and become cooked rice, then they might follow and practice it. The Master said:
How laughable is this ignorance! How extreme is this perversion! Your innate goodness is clear and unerring; you silently accord with the will of Heaven. Spirits rejoice and people are glad;
as harmony is invoked, auspicious blessings naturally follow. A poem says: "Happy indeed is the noble one; may fortune and rank be extended to him.

If one were to claim that virtue leads to loss while wealth brings gain, or that integrity results in poverty while depravity yields riches, one would instead be slandering the innate mind as useless and incapable.

They enter the cauldron. Little do they realize that the Way of Heaven has already been obscured; in secret, the spirits resent and the ghosts rage, diminishing their blessings and robbing them of their longevity.
Poverty, exhaustion, and calamities follow, even to the point that their descendants become unworthy. There is no strange misfortune that does not occur. As the *Wenchang Shu* says:

"To those who cultivate themselves and exert themselves in practice, Heaven will surely bestow a hundred auspicious signs. To those who oppose the Way and ruin their virtue, the spirits shall likewise take away their five blessings."
Thus one knows that the principle of blessings for goodness and calamity for lust is an inevitable and certain law.

If one is willing to reform evil and practice good, without deceiving or obscuring oneself, then Buddhas and deities will naturally provide secret protection, and one's fortune and longevity will increase.
The worldly saying goes: "If one can reform their faults, is that not permissible? The Master said: "Who is without fault? Who is without transgression?
To know one's faults and reform them—nothing is more virtuous than this. Faults and evils are manifold, pertaining to body, mind, and speech;
one must remain constantly alert and examine oneself at every moment. Whether what one does is appropriate or inappropriate, if it is good, then act upon it."

If you commit an evil, correct it immediately. To reform evil and follow good is like a patient breaking a sweat; naturally, there will be auspiciousness and blessings, and the various sages will protect you. As the worldly saying goes:
"Even if one’s oversight fails for a moment and thoughts arise in the mind, how does one subdue that mind?
The Master said: "The ancients governed their minds by guarding against the slightest [faults], and thus their achievements were immense. Whether the human heart is good or evil,"

There is nothing that does not arise from thought. When thought moves, be quick to awaken; once awakened, it vanishes. By repeatedly withdrawing and gathering [the mind], the mind naturally becomes upright.
As the Book says: "Lacking mindfulness leads to madness; being able to maintain mindfulness leads to sagehood. These are the ultimate words; follow them and act accordingly.
A layperson asked: "Those living at home are entangled by the five desires and cannot suddenly escape them. I do not know what skillful means there might be to allow for gradual cultivation.
The Master said: "Cultivation while living at home is the most difficult of all matters; one must possess courageous vigor, firm resolve, and constant perseverance."
Whether in motion or stillness, amidst the busyness or leisure of daily life, simply hold up the single phrase "Amitābha Buddha.
Turn the light back upon itself and maintain this single thought-moment alone. Even if a wheel of fire were to spin above your head, you must certainly not abandon this single thought-moment;
even if the eight winds should all come together to buffet you, do not lose this single thought-moment. As days pass and months deepen, this single thought-moment—
Be pure and sincere. Once again, shatter that single thought; only then will the Amitābha of one’s own nature manifest.

Should you fail to attain awakening during this lifetime, at the moment your retribution ends and your life concludes, maintain that single thought and proceed directly upon the right path. Upon returning, you shall hear it once more and awaken to a thousand truths.
To see one's nature and attain Buddhahood is within one's reach; this is the essential point for returning to the heart. For now, do not seek outwardly.
Only when your own words and deeds are without flaw can it be called true enjoyment.

In the discourse on the principles of Confucianism and Buddhism, the Confucians say that the Way of the Buddhists lacks reverence for father and ruler, and that the evaluations of former scholars liken them to Yang Zhu and Mo Di.

Having investigated this closely myself, I find they are indeed correct. The Master said: "When the Buddha was on the path of practice, throughout immeasurable kalpas, he gouged out his own eyes to save his parents."
Sacrificing one’s body to save one’s father and extensively practicing loyalty and filial piety cannot fully repay such kindness;

only by leaving the household life, studying the unsurpassed path, and attaining equal and perfect enlightenment can one finally fulfill the debt of gratitude. As the Buddhist sutras say: "If a person serves their parents with filial piety, the Lord of Devas, Śakra, resides within that person's home.
If they provide filial support to their parents, the Great Brahma, the Honored Deva, resides within that person's home. Furthermore, if one is able to practice filial piety...
Revere your parents; the Buddhas reside within your home. The Buddha’s Vinaya states: "Filial piety is called the precept. It further says:
"One who practices giving without first making offerings to their parents is called an evil person. A verse by Maitreya says: "There are two Buddhas in the hall above;
alas, the people of this world do not recognize them. They are not fashioned with gold and pigments, nor are they carved from sandalwood."
[This is] an inscription. Those who are currently our parents are none other than Śākyamuni and Maitreya. If one can revere them with a sincere heart, what need is there to seek merit elsewhere?

Although the Buddha’s teachings contain no words regarding the governance of a state, they are able to lead the people toward goodness and transform the world, converting the heterodox to the orthodox.
They cause the ignorant masses to practice all manner of virtues and enable the wise to awaken to principle and cultivate their minds; this may truly be called "enlightened."

To propagate the Buddha-way is truly to secretly repay the Imperial Grace. Have you not seen that the sons of the Śākya in the monasteries throughout the land recite their liturgies morning and evening to repay the four debts of gratitude and provide sustenance for all beings in the three realms of existence?

If one’s heart were deficient toward the Buddha, being neither loyal nor filial, how could the Bodhisattvas of the ten directions, the Arhats whose outflows are exhausted, the eight classes of devas and nagas, and the various spirits of every path ever deign to take refuge [in them]?
I rely on you to assist me with a sincere heart; how could I speak falsely? You should examine this for yourself. The Confucians say:
"When one's parents are alive, one does not travel far. Even distant travel is not permitted, let alone mutilating one's appearance and separating from one's kin.

The Master said: "You know only the small filial piety of the mundane world, but you do not realize the great filial piety that transcends the world. Filial piety within the world must not be abandoned:

serve one's parents with propriety while they are alive, bury them with propriety when they die, and offer sacrifices to them with propriety thereafter. Thus, the way of filiality is fully perfected from beginning to end.
The Confucian teachings know only how to serve and be filial toward one's parents; they do not know what to do for parents who have passed away."

As for one's present parents, if they have created karma and fallen into the three miserable realms as a result of their retribution, yet their child succeeds in leaving the household life and suddenly realizes unsurpassed *bodhi*, thereby being able to rescue them from suffering, this can be called truly repaying the kindness of one's parents. As an ancient worthy said:

"If one child leaves the household life, the nine ancestors ascend to heaven. Although a monk has altered his physical form, it is said that he has distanced himself from the secular world to study [the Way].
The Way is easily accomplished by one who does not maintain a wife or children; this may be called severing the bonds of affection and swiftly attaining perfect enlightenment.
You yourself know the five relationships of the world, yet you do not know the supreme filial piety of saving one's parents.

The Confucianist says: "Among the three forms of unfiliality, having no descendants is the greatest. The Master said: "In the worldly order of human relations, failing to continue one's lineage is indeed unfilial;
however, in the supramundane Way, it is not included among such faults. The continuity of sentient beings has craving as its cause; because they do not cease their attachment, they remain bound."
Like glue and lacquer, they gather together life after life and remain entangled from generation to generation; parents and children come and go without interruption.
If one possesses true wisdom, with resolute determination and fierce courage, and exerts great valor to sever the bonds of craving and desire, one will suddenly awaken to the nature of the mind.

One directly transcends to the stage of awakening. Although the lineage is severed, this does not constitute a transgression; there is a transcendental filial piety of its own that truly repays the kindness of one's ancestors.
As the Confucians say: "The clergy, as soon as they open their mouths, speak of transcendence. If there were indeed such a Dharma of transcendence, it would have to be otherwise... [not so].
"To walk in the world" means to walk within the world as it exists now. Why then speak of "transcending the world"? The Master said:
"A student of the Way does not become defiled by worldly conditions; being liberated in every situation is called 'transcending the world. It does not mean departing from the world."
There is another way to emerge [from the world]. For example, when those of the Confucian school pass the examinations, it is said that they have "ascended the dragon" or "broken the cassia branch.
Yet, how could there truly be a dragon to ride upon or a cassia branch to grasp? It is laughable that those who are deluded by their attachments instead give rise to such heterodox views.
The Confucianist said, "I see that members of the monastic community are greedy for fame and pursue profit, practicing nothing but worldly dharmas; how have they ever been free from defilement?

The Master said, "In this age of the Dharma’s decline, we are far removed from the sages. Dragons and snakes are intermingled, and ordinary people and sages walk side by side. Even if there were wise men," [the Confucianist continued,] "..."
It is nothing other than worldly dharmas. To practice what is not the Way and yet achieve the Buddha-way is difficult for the fleshly eye to discern;

do not give rise to superficial judgments. The Confucianist says: "The Sage Confucius attacked the doctrines of heterodox schools. Are these not precisely the teachings of the two schools of Buddhism and Daoism? The Master said:
If Confucius had considered Laozi a heterodox teacher, there would have been the lament regarding his seeking the rites from Lao Dan.
If he had considered Buddhism a heterodox teaching, such a view could not have existed at that time, as the Buddha-dharma had not yet arrived.

Rather, because Confucius observed during the Spring and Autumn period that the worthy were excessive while the foolish were deficient—both failing to attain the Middle Way—he referred to them as "heterodox. Later scholars merely borrowed this term to slander the Buddhists and Daoists.
Second, as for the teachings: their explanations are fragmented and do not reach the Great Way.
The Confucians say that the Buddha’s doctrine of cessation is a heterodox teaching; the former Confucian scholars have examined this and found their assessment to be correct. The Master said:
That which is called "quiescence" is not a quiescence that exists in opposition to movement; from the beginningless past, it has been fundamentally unmoving quiescence.
That which is called "extinction" is not an extinction that exists in opposition to arising; from the beginningless past, it has been fundamentally the extinction of no-arising-and-no-extinction.

This is the entire substance of the original nature, from which all manifold functions are issued. Later Confucianists, failing to awaken to the substance of this nature, recklessly give rise to notions of annihilation and cessation.
This is a different view. The Confucians say: "Our Confucianism exhausts principle and fully realizes human nature; it is not like the biased emptiness of Buddhism. The Master said:

"The Buddha says that when quiescence is manifested before one, the six sense organs function interchangeably. The Confucians say: 'It is silent and unmoving, yet when stimulated, it penetrates all things. The Buddha speaks of *tathatā* (suchness)."
It is immovable. The Confucian says it is "empty and void. The Buddhist transforms consciousness into wisdom; Yan Hui, in his study of sagehood, was repeatedly empty.
If one regards such quiescent extinction as a heterodox teaching, then Confucius’s state of emptiness is no different from that of the Buddha.

Later Confucians did not understand the substance of nature and groundlessly and falsely discoursed on partial emptiness. Only upon awakening to the state prior to the arousal of thoughts will one know that Confucianism and Buddhism are non-dual.

The Confucians say: "The Buddhists constantly use cause and effect to terrify the ignorant masses, claiming that if a person is good they will surely be born in heaven, while if they are evil they will certainly fall into hell.
The cycle of the six realms and the karmic retributions of the three paths are such empty fabrications."
This is the height of deluding people. How could the followers of the Buddha know that after a person’s life ends, the breath transforms into a pure wind and the physical body turns to mud?
One lifetime has already ceased; who comes back again? The Master said: "There is neither cause nor effect. Heaven and hell are entirely false.
A person lives one lifetime and upon death returns to nothingness. The breath transforms into a pure wind, and the flesh turns to mud—just as you [have described]."
Regarding this doctrine: since there is neither cause nor effect, the *I Ching* says, "In a family that accumulates goodness, there will surely be an abundance of blessings;
in a family that accumulates evil, there will surely be an abundance of calamities. Furthermore, the *Book of Documents* says, "For those who do good, a hundred auspicious signs descend upon them;
for those who do evil, a hundred calamities descend upon them. If there is no hell, why does the tradition say that one who commits evil in the realm of the unseen will be met by ghosts?
The divine spirits will find and punish them. Since there is no transmigration, for what reason do you further say that those who die here are reborn there?
All things emerge from the mechanism [of fate] and all enter back into the mechanism. If there were no retribution for causes and effects, human life would merely be a single lifetime;
it would be best to indulge in dissipation and act recklessly according to one's whims. After death, one would simply become a breeze amidst the clear air. From oneself—
Setting aside for a moment the analogy of the wind as a transformation, it follows that the pure breeze is insentient and fundamentally lacks cognition.
Cheng Hao said: "When a filial son sacrifices to his ancestors, their spirits descend; this is because the utmost sincerity has a resonance that necessarily penetrates.
Regarding such a statement, when the ancestors descend, do they descend as the pure breeze, or do they descend as spiritual consciousness? If they descend as spiritual consciousness, [then...]

The spiritual essence becomes wind. If this is the clear breeze that comes, the clear breeze is insentient. Is it not the case that after the ancestors have died, their nature transforms into insentient wind?
When descendants offer sacrifices to them, it again changes back into a spiritual essence; after receiving the sacrifice, it transforms once more into a clear breeze.
Such coming and going, such transformations—truly a wondrous wind! Chengzi further said: "The ghost is the departed..."

Yet they do not reflect upon the meaning of this. Since it is already the case that [the spirits] go and do not return, that the descendants can move them through their utmost sincerity is, moreover, a matter of "returning.
This is truly laughable. Yichuan said: "Ghosts and spirits are the sublime functioning of the two qi.
Yang qi ascends to heaven as spirits; yin qi descends to earth as ghosts. He further stated that cause and effect are provisional, and that paradise and hell are not real.
Yang-energy arising in heaven becomes the divine; Yin-energy descending to earth becomes the ghostly. Furthermore, these fall within the sphere of cause and effect and responsive resonance.

One cannot help but lament that the worldly Confucian scholars do not awaken to the wondrous nature—which is neither existent nor non-existent, neither born nor extinguished—yet falsely conceive of it as undergoing annihilation.

Having personally obscured one's own original truth, one must swiftly give rise to wisdom. One must urgently seek out an enlightened teacher and be willing to request even a single word or half-phrase to illuminate the Way of the Single Thread.
Thus, one will certainly not fall into the two views of annihilationism and eternalism, and will fully realize the principle of "Middle Harmony" within the Confucian school.

The Confucianist said, "Since cause and effect are never obscured and the retribution for good and evil is without error, why was Emperor Wu—who venerated the Buddha—still beset by the calamity of Hou Jing that led to the ruin of his state?
The Master replied, "The length of a dynasty's mandate and the order or chaos of its successive reigns—"
All things have a fixed number; therefore, they cannot be altered. Emperor Wu of Liang adhered to the Hīnayāna, specializing exclusively in conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).

He placed excessive faith in the traces of the mud and clung to the Middle Way without skillful means (*upāya*). When Hou Jing’s army arrived, he failed to employ expedient means, instead assembling a multitude of śramaṇas to shake bells and strike chimes.
Contemplate the Mahāprajñāpāramitā. For example, during the Later Han dynasty, when Xiang Xu was faced with the rebellion of Zhang Jiao, he did not wish for the state to mobilize its armies;
instead, he merely pursued the rebel troops to the riverbank and recited the *Classic of Filial Piety* facing north. When the rebels heard this, they were naturally dispersed.
The employment of such unwholesome dharmas—how could this be the fault of the *Xiaojing*? Emperor Wu of Liang adhered to the Middle Way, yet his fixed karma led to the ruin of his state;
it was not caused by performing good deeds that diminished his fortune. Emperor Wu reached an advanced age of ninety, and his fixed karma resulted in his death due to illness.
"It would not lead to great evil. Why, then, do you rely on this to slander the holy teaching and bring only blame upon yourself?

The Confucianist said, "The Master says that fixed karma is difficult to escape; as for the matter of spiritual resonance, its truth or falsehood remains uncertain. The Master replied, "It is the karma created in previous lives."
Receiving retribution in this life, cultivating merit in this very body, and experiencing happiness upon returning—this principle is fixed; it cannot be altered by oneself.

Emperor Wu contracted enmity during his lifetime, and thus met with a long-standing feud in this world. Although he encountered such grievous suffering, the causes of goodness he cultivated will bear fruit in a future life;
the resulting joy shall certainly not be obscured.
The Confucian said, "Cause and effect are not obscure; they are fixed and cannot be altered. The Master said, "This is the law of certainty.

Yet, is there anything uncertain? The Confucian asked, "How can it be uncertain? The Master replied, "One may have committed karma in a previous life and yet suffer poverty and an early death in this life.

Or, by practicing benevolent deeds, one's sins may be extinguished and blessings may arise. Or, having contracted a debt of life in a past kalpa, one encounters the creditor in this life due to the actions performed."
"Virtuous One, [this power] moves heaven and earth and transforms the ominous into the auspicious. An ancient worthy said: 'If one practices hidden virtue, one can resolve past karma.
Although there are fixed laws, there are also those that are not fixed."
The Confucianist said: "Emperor Wu surrendered his body [to the monastic community], repaired temples, erected stupas, printed scriptures, fashioned images, honored the Buddha, and ordained monks.

For such goodness, how could there not be hidden virtue (*yin-de*) that moves heaven and earth, resolves grievances, and releases one from calamity? The Master said: "This is a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) based on conditioned action (*saṃskṛta*);
it will result in the experience of pleasant fruits once again. However, as for hidden virtue performed without a [discursive] mind, it can unite with the Mind of Heaven."
This is why it can transform the ominous into the auspicious and turn calamity into fortune.
A Confucianist says: "If the Buddha-dharma were correct and identical to Confucian principles, why did Ouyang Xiu say that the Buddha is a great affliction for China?
The Master said: "If the Buddha-dharma were not correct and were indeed a great affliction for China, why [did he say so]?"

From ancient times until the present day, from sage emperors and worthy kings to ministers, great scholars, elders, lay devotees, nuns, and servant girls, those who revere the Buddha are as numerous as the surging tides, and those who take refuge in him are like stars surrounding the North Star.

How could it be that among them there is not a single person who recognizes this as heterodoxy and eliminates it? This is all the more so since the Buddha is far away and his physical presence has not yet arrived here.
Yet, without relying on verbal teachings, this has been transmitted to this land. If it were a doctrine that harms people, how could it have been allowed to circulate for so long?
Why would people not grow weary of it? Heaven ought to punish it.

The Confucianist says: "Ouyang Xiu stated that Buddhists are skilled at performing unverified and unreal acts of giving. The Master said: "If the Buddha’s acts of giving were merely false, there must be some ulterior motive behind them.
If you say it was for fame and profit, the Buddha was originally most noble. If you say it was to escape hunger and cold, the Buddha was originally most wealthy.
Why, then, did he renounce his sovereign throne of wealth and honor, instead performing these unverified and unreal acts that delude people? This, too..."

How extremely perverse and strange this is! If the Buddha possessed even the slightest trace of deceitful or false intent, how could the sages and worthies of the ten directions have been willing to follow him in propagating the teachings?
As the Sūtra says: "The Tathāgata speaks the true word, speaks the real word, and speaks according to reality."
"Those who do not speak deceptively and those who do not speak falsely—these are merely the words of Ou-yang Hsiu’s deluded mind.
The Confucianists say: Han Yü stated that Buddhism is but one teaching from the Western Regions that flowed into China during the Later Han dynasty;
it did not exist in antiquity. From the time of the Yellow Emperor down to the reigns of Wen and Wu, there were none [who followed it], certainly not more than a hundred."
"Years! As for those who served the Buddha in later generations, their devotion gradually became more earnest, yet the duration of their lifespans remained short. How pitiful!

The Master said, "When Great Sages descend into the world, they are not restricted by location, nor are they restricted by the length of their lifespan. Among the emperors of China, Emperor Shun was born at Zhufeng and died at Mingtiao;
he was a man of the eastern lands. King Wen was born at Qizhou and died at Biying; he was a man of the western lands. Thus it was with Shun..."
Both [the kings] and King Wen were sages who served as models for the world; later generations revered them, and each attained their respective lifespans according to their station.
If one claims that people lived long in antiquity but their lives became shortened in later ages due to practicing Buddhism, why were the reigns of Wang Waibing and Zhongren so brief?
And why did Kong Li and Yan Yuan not live much longer? Truly, this is due to the causes of one's own goodness.

To claim that serving the Buddha shortens one's lifespan, while asserting that Han Yu’s slander of the Buddha ought to result in eternal longevity— such arguments, which are like covering one's ears while stealing a bell,
cannot escape the laughter of the wise.
The Confucian said, "In Buddhism, they speak of 'clarifying the mind and seeing one's nature,' and 'seeing one's nature to achieve Buddhahood. Our Confucians have never had such unreal talk.
The Master said, "Buddhism teaches people to clarify the mind and see their nature, and to see their nature to achieve Buddhahood.
Mencius said, 'Exhaust your mind and you will know your nature; knowing your nature, you will know Heaven. He also said that one should recite the words of Yao and act as Yao did."
To practice such conduct is to be merely Yao. To awaken to the words of the Buddha and practice the conduct of the Buddha is to be merely the Buddha.
What difference is there between Confucianism and Buddhism? Yet you claim that [my] words are not true.

The Confucian said, "Since one has awakened to the words of the Buddha, one must certainly practice the deeds of the Buddha. Yet, I observe that among the monastics there are many who do not follow the Buddha's precepts;
what is the reason for this? The Master replied, "The Dharma-gate is vast and expansive; dragons and snakes are intermingled therein."
During the Buddha’s lifetime, there were still the six groups of bhikṣus; how much more so now in the age of the Dharma’s decay, when we are ever further removed from the Sage?
Among the thousands and tens of thousands of śākyaputrīyas today, it would be enough to find but one who even resembles an ancient worthy. It is like sifting sand to select gold:
from ten *hù* of sand, a single grain is found that becomes a treasure for the world. Or it is like piling stones to grind jade: [one grain of jade from a mountain of rock].
Regarding the stones of a mountain: even obtaining an inch of jade makes it a precious treasure. As the ancient masters said: "Though there be many horns, a single qilin suffices.

It is not only during this age of the Dharma’s decline that such individuals are difficult to find within Buddhism; even in the time of Confucius, there were already those who were "scholars of the gentleman" and those who were "scholars of the petty man.
As for those who currently wear the robes of a Confucian scholar, how can one guarantee that they all truly embody the character of Confucius?
Mengzi said: "This is why the teachings of the Semblance Dharma are not confined solely to the monastic community, nor is there a lack of discipline among them; Confucianism is likewise no exception.

The Confucians say: 'Since the three teachings share a single principle, why do you falsely distinguish between their ranks? Buddhism treats the marrow and bones, while Daoism [treats the flesh and blood]...'"
“The teachings of our school treat the blood vessels; Confucianism treats the skin and surface. Such unbalanced statements cannot help but provoke anger in people.

The Master said, “In the Confucian gate, taking the investigation of principle and the perfection of nature as the Way, and the Three Bonds and Five Constants as virtue, they seek to make people into gentlemen;
thus, they treat the skin and surface. In the Daoist school, taking the cultivation of the Real and the nourishment of nature as the Way, and the weakening of the will [as the method]...”
To withdraw from worldly affairs for the sake of virtue makes one a pure and empty Daoist; thus it is said that such a person "treats the blood vessels.

Buddhism takes the illumination of the mind and realization of its nature as the Way (*dào*), and the ten perfections and myriad practices as virtue. To achieve perfect enlightenment and become a teacher of the three realms is truly to "treat the marrow and bones.
It is not that the essential substance of the Way differs among these three teachings; rather, it is because the meritorious practices of each school differ.
A Confucian asked, "How can it be said that the three teachings share a single essence? The Master replied, "In terms of their essence, they are one:

the Buddhist teaching is the seeing of nature, the Daoist teaching is the nourishing of nature, and the Confucian teaching is the exhausting of nature. Although the gateways through which one enters differ, the source to which they return is non-dual."
The Confucianist said, "The Buddhist teachings and those of the Confucians are not the same. The Master asked, "In what way are they different?
The Confucianist replied, "In our teaching, one first studies the texts and then lectures upon them; by extensively reading the various books, one exhausts the principles of human nature and emotion.

In the Buddhist gate, one is first taught to practice seated meditation and investigate the *huatou* (critical phrase) to awaken to the Way of the mind-nature. Therefore, there is a great difference between Buddhism and Confucianism. The Master said:
That which enters from without is not one's own treasure; that which arises from within is alone called true wisdom.

At that time, among the disciples of Confucius, only Yan Hui attained awakening; the others, though possessing much learning and broad vision, all relied on external factors to stimulate their understanding.
Therefore, there is a difference as vast as that between heaven and earth between learning and awakening.

For example, Cheng Mingdao received instruction from Mu Shu, who constantly directed him to investigate the source of the joy experienced by Zhongni (Confucius) and Yanzi. Is this "joy of Zhongni and Yanzi" not itself a *huatou*?
Furthermore, Luo Zhongsu of Yuzhang taught people only to sit in stillness and engage in investigation, focusing on the state when the four beginnings have not yet been manifested.

What a magnificent state! Not only does it provide power for advancing in learning, but it is also essential for cultivating the mind. These two gentlemen were eminent worthies of the Confucian school;
how are they different from those of the Chan school who engage in investigation and attain awakening?
The Confucian said, "I cannot believe in the principle of sudden enlightenment. The Master replied, "Not only do the Confucian beginners of today lack faith in it;
even the worthy disciples of the Confucian school, such as Zigong and Zizhang, lacked faith in it.
At that time, only Yanzi believed in it, which is why Confucius praised him for his love of learning."
The Confucianist says: "Our teaching enters through practice; by acting, one accords with principle. The Buddhist enters through principle; by sitting in stillness, one awakens to principle.
Therefore, those who accord with principle while acting possess great power, whereas those who awaken to principle through sitting in stillness possess weak power."
The Master said: "What you have said is indeed correct in principle; yet there is nothing one can do about the fact that what is familiar is too familiar and what is raw is too raw.
If a student, while amidst movement, realizes the principle within their familiar ground and does not deviate from it due to external circumstances, such a case occurs but once in ten thousand.

Beginners tend to lean toward stillness; if they refine this raw state until it is perfected, they will naturally gain power when they encounter movement. When Li Ao (Yichuan) saw someone sitting in meditation..."
I rejoice that this person has learned well. Zhu Xi said: "The Way teaches people to practice quiet sitting; Master Li also taught people to practice quiet sitting.
This is because if the spirit is not settled, the Way will have no place to settle. If one can cultivate it through quiet sitting..."

This is truly refreshing. As for the various scholars mentioned above, they were skilled in loving stillness and pursuing investigation; this is laughable when compared to the secular scholars of the present day.

Their deluded minds undergo birth and cessation without a moment's rest; when confronted by objects or meeting with conditions, they lack any sense of mastery. How can such people engage in the practice?
This movement accords with the Way of the Single Thread.

What the Confucians call "the ultimate principle" and what the Chan practitioners call "a single word that transforms the ordinary into the sage"—such wondrous marvels make it difficult for Confucians to believe.

The Master said: "At that time, Zeng Shen’s pursuit of principle was so earnest that when he suddenly heard Confucius say, 'I penetrate all things with one,' he immediately attained realization of the principle of mind and nature.
Furthermore, Zhou Maoshu told his disciples, 'The weeds in front of the hall have not been cleared.
When someone asked the meaning of this, he replied, 'It is just like my own state of mind. Zhang Zithou attained understanding upon hearing the bray of a donkey."
This is not merely a single word of ultimate principle; it is the very model of transforming the ordinary into the sacred.
The Confucians say that the Chan school uses karmic conditions for verification, whereas we Confucians certainly have no such practice. The Master said:
"In the past, when Cheng Yichuan saw Shao Kangjie, Cheng pointed to the dining table and asked Shao, 'This table is placed upon the ground.'"
One does not know where heaven and earth truly reside. Mr. Kangjie discussed this principle at great length; this very question serves as a karmic occasion for verification.

The Confucians say: "We teach our various disciples, yet all their discourses on the *wuji* (Ultimate Non-being) and *taiji* (Supreme Ultimate) fail to provide clear and lucid understanding. Thus, the later students were, for a time, left in confusion.

"It is difficult to enter. The Master explained that the three teachings share a single principle. "Why do you not extend a hand and eye to turn those who have not yet awakened? To believe in the Buddha is supreme. The Master said:

"The two teachings of Daoism and Confucianism are largely identical in their principles. From the Ultimate Non-being (*wuji*) arises the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*). The Supreme Ultimate moves and gives birth to Yang;
when movement reaches its limit, it becomes still, and from stillness, Yin is born. One Yin and one Yang—the two polarities (*liangyi*)—interact with one another."

The four images and five elements give rise to the myriad things; yet, although you have generally reasoned to the ultimate limit, you still do not recognize that these are manifestations of this mind.
If I were to show you that they are fundamentally pure and serene, you might wonder how mountains, rivers, and the great earth could suddenly arise from them.

Fearing that you would find it difficult to enter [this truth], I have provisionally borrowed the two distinct principles of the "Ultimate" and the "Supreme Ultimate" from Confucianism to make your awakening easier. Investigate this further.
The Buddha-vehicle is the ultimate limit (*anuttara*) when its original nature is empty and quiescent; it is the Great Ultimate (*taiji*) when the true mind is luminously aware.

Quiescence and illumination are non-dual, like a mirror reflecting objects: it can distinguish good from evil without giving rise to discrimination. Yet, as soon as a thought-stirring impulse (*xinji*) begins to sprout, good and evil become chaotic.

Just as the Grand Ultimate (Taiji) moves to give rise to Yin and Yang, and Yin and Yang interact with one another to produce the myriad things, so too does the True Mind respond to objects without giving rise to discrimination.
As soon as a single thought arises, the myriad dharmas manifest simultaneously. Thus, by metaphorically pointing to the nature of mind, the Way of Change (Yidao) is elucidated.
"If you go to the Chan Gate, you must study there for another thirty years.

The Confucian said, "I teach the *Doctrine of the Mean* and the *Great Learning*, which are called the Classics of the Sages. Would you, Master, not begrudge me a single explanation? The Master replied:
The Way of the Great Learning consists in making bright the luminous virtue, in bringing the people near, and in resting in ultimate goodness. The commentary states:

The Way of the Great Learning in the school of Confucius does not refer to ritual, music, archery, or calligraphy; it does not fall into the extremes of excess or deficiency, but abides in the principle of the Middle Way.
"Making bright the luminous virtue" is explained in two ways: the former refers to awakening, and the latter refers to the mind—the true mind.
Vast and spiritual, it illuminates while remaining eternally quiescent. "Virtue" refers to the functional activity of the mind, which is purely good and devoid of evil.

The Three Bonds and Five Constants, as well as ritual, music, law, and governance, all emerge from the functional activity of this wondrously luminous, single mind. Furthermore, because sentient beings since time immemorial have pursued external objects and followed their emotions, they have been defiled for a long duration;
thus, they have turned their backs on the functional activity of virtue, becoming inverted and confused, obscuring their inherent clarity and drifting away.
Regarding birth and death: once one awakens to and clarifies the original mind, one will finally know that the worthy and the ignorant are no different.
After attaining self-awakening, one must transform others, causing every person to manifest the wondrously luminous true mind and to practice this so as to reach the ground of ultimate goodness.
The above constitutes sudden enlightenment; what follows concerns cultivation and realization. "Only after knowing where to rest does one attain stability;

only after stability can one attain tranquility; only after tranquility can one attain serenity; only after serenity can one attain deliberation; only after deliberation can one attain attainment. The commentary states:
