One knows for oneself that one must come to rest in the state of ultimate goodness. Ultimate goodness is the principle of the Middle Way. If one comes to rest in the Middle Way, [attainment follows].
Naturally, one will have no delusions regarding good and evil; this may be called "knowing when to stop, after which there is stability.
Stability means the mind does not move; external things cannot shift it. When one reaches the point where things cannot shift it, the original mind is like a bright mirror:
pure, responding to objects without being stained. This is called "stability, after which one can attain tranquility. Tranquility refers to the tranquility of the original mind; it is not—

To still the movement within stillness is true stillness; when one moves forward into this true stillness, there is no obstruction anywhere. If one reaches the state where there is no obstruction anywhere, then movement and shaking will naturally be without disorder.
If there is shaking without disorder, it is called true peace (*an*). Therefore, it is said that "only after attaining stillness can one attain peace.
Peace means being at ease and leisurely; inner and outer are as one. One proceeds spontaneously with stability and composure, acting with reality in all affairs. Thus ends the passage.
This is always concentration (*samādhi*). What follows may be called wisdom (*prajñā*). If the fruit of concentration is still, peaceful, and enduring, true wisdom will naturally manifest.
This is why it is said that "only after being settled can one deliberate. Deliberation is true wisdom; therein, all things are without obstruction.
If one reaches the state where phenomena and phenomena are mutually unimpeded, it may be said that one is able to attain [the goal] through deliberation.

To "attain" means to attain non-attainment; this is simply the equality of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). Things have their roots and branches; affairs have their beginnings and ends. To know what comes first and what follows is to draw near to the Way.
The commentary states: "To illumine one's own luminous virtue" is called the root; "to transform others and clarify principles" is called the branch.
To know when to stop and reach ultimate goodness may be called the beginning. Later, returning to the fundamental mind is called the end; thus, from beginning to end, the sequence is unerring.
Naturally, one draws near to the Way of the Great Learning. Those of antiquity who wished to illuminate their virtue throughout the world first brought order to their states.
Those who wished to bring order to their states first brought harmony to their families. Those who wished to bring harmony to their families...
First cultivate the person. One who wishes to cultivate the person must first rectify the mind. One who wishes to rectify the mind must first make the intention sincere.
One who wishes to make the intention sincere must first extend knowledge. Extending knowledge lies in the investigation of things. The commentary states:
Ancient rulers, having realized the root, governed the branches. To govern the people of the world, they first had to govern a single state. To govern...

To bring order to a state, one must first bring order to the family. If one wishes to require an entire family to study and practice this principle, one must first cultivate the virtue of one's own person.
If one cultivates the virtue of one's person, one must first rectify the mind. The mind is originally without depravity; it becomes so because of the movement of the will.
The mind's intentions are inverted and involve deception and falsehood. That which is called "rectifying the heart" must first require "sincerizing the intention.

Sincerity means being true and real; it responds to things without partiality. To desire that one's response to things be without partiality, one must first bring forth one's innate knowledge (*liangzhi*).
Innate knowledge (*liangzhi*) is the spiritual luminosity of the mind; it is like a mirror reflecting objects without giving rise to discrimination.

Now, because one discriminates between hatred and love, this is merely the deluded capacity of emotional consciousness (*qing-shi*). Therefore, it is said that "to bring innate knowledge to fulfillment requires the investigation of things" (*gewu*).
Here, "things" refers to emotional consciousness, not external objects. As the Buddha said: "If one can master things, one is identical to the Tathāgata. Later Confucians failed to realize this.

Things are fundamentally rooted in one's own consciousness; yet people mistakenly take "investigating things" (*gewu*) to mean the exhaustive inquiry into external objects, desiring to reach their ultimate limits so that there is nothing to which they do not penetrate.

It is lamentable that such outward seeking only serves to further delude them by the objects themselves. Only after things are investigated does knowledge become perfected; only after knowledge is perfected does the will become sincere; only after the will is sincere does the mind become correct;
only after the mind is correct does the person cultivate themselves; only after the person has cultivated themselves can the family be brought to order. Once the family is ordered...
Thereafter the state is governed; when the state is governed, all under heaven is at peace. The commentary states: This section of text returns to the original intent.

If one can transform consciousness, innate knowing (*liangzhi*) will spontaneously arrive. When innate knowing manifests, it is like a mirror reflecting objects; good and evil are clearly distinguished, and neither hatred nor attachment arises.
When hatred and attachment do not arise, the mind is sincere and free from partiality. When the mind is sincere and free from partiality, the spirit is born without [obstruction].
Delusion. With a correct mind and upright body, one acts in accordance with the natural principle; whatever is done spontaneously accords with the Ultimate Way.
Thus, I have moved and transformed my family, and they all study my practice; I have moved and transformed my country, and they all listen to my instructions.
Consequently, the people of the world have all become good and virtuous—from the Son of Heaven down to the commoners—all are unified in their cultivation of the self.

The self is the root. It is impossible for the branches to be well-ordered while the root is in disorder. It has never happened that what is most substantial is treated with scant regard, while what is trivial is treated with great weight.
The commentary states: From the Son of Heaven above to the common people below, all take the single mind as their fundamental basis.
Not only is the mind the root of the individual body; it can also serve as the foundation for both transcending the world and governing the world.
The Foundation. If this foundation is disordered, then cultivating oneself, regulating the family, governing the state, and bringing peace to the world will not be possible;

such a thing has never occurred. The Confucian said: "I have already heard the *Great Learning*; please show me the *Doctrine of the Mean*. The Master said: "What Heaven mandates is called nature (*xing*). To follow nature..."

This refers to the Way. The cultivation of the Way is what is called "teaching. The commentary states: Regarding the mind-teachings of the Confucian school, the principle of the *Zhongyong* (The Doctrine of the Mean) is to be neither biased nor leaning, neither deviant nor stagnant.
Zhu Xi’s sub-commentary explains that "nature" is like the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*), which is bestowed upon all things and persons, each being granted its own principle.
It is not yet known what kind of entity this original nature is; it is as if the mandate of Heaven has come to be entrusted to persons and things. Yet, one takes this [Confucian]...

The principle of the Sage is annotated as follows: [He claims] that there are phenomena external to the mind; how could he know the fundamental nature? Its essence is like the great void—without interior or exterior, neither coming nor going.
It is entirely because, at the very beginning, one failed to maintain one's own nature and suddenly gave rise to a stirring mind that one undergoes the prison of the womb.
What was originally a single brilliant spirit is divided into six functions; following objects and pursuing emotions, it drifts through birth and death. Sentient beings do not...
One can return to the source. The former sages pointed out the direct path and extracted that the mandate of Heaven (*tianming*) is precisely the essence of nature (*xingti*).

The mandate of Heaven, the mind of Heaven, the Way of Heaven, and the principle of Heaven—though their names differ, their substance is identical; they are all, in total, the principle of nature (*xingli*). As an ancient worthy said: "In relation to Heaven, it is called the mandate."
In humans, this is called "nature" (*xing*). Therefore, it is shown [in the *Doctrine of the Mean*]: "That which Heaven mandates is called nature.

From the very beginning, every person is inherently endowed with a single, wondrously luminous, true nature that responds spontaneously to circumstances. This principle is naturally so; within its essence, its function is harmonious, never falling into partiality or bias.
In the affairs of daily life, phenomena and principle are unimpeded; hence it is said: "To follow one's nature is called the Way (*dao*). All of this is due to the process of receiving birth.

Dust-like defilements arise, obscuring the fundamental principle. Through inverted and chaotic thoughts, one fails to awaken to the essence of nature. Thus, the sages established teachings to transform people so they may restore their original nature;
by awakening to the principle and practicing its realization, one turns back from delusion to return to the truth, thereby restoring the principle of one's original heavenly mandate.
This is what is meant by "teaching" as the cultivation of the Way. Teaching is the cultivation of the Way, and the Way is rooted in nature; the source of the essence of nature is...
Regarding Heaven: the sage rejoices in Heaven and knows his destiny; this is the Way of the Mean. This Way cannot be departed from for even a moment;
that which can be departed from is not the Way. Therefore, the noble person is cautious and reverent in what is unseen, and fearful and apprehensive in what is unheard.
Nothing is more manifest than that which is hidden; nothing is more evident than that which is subtle. Thus, the noble person must certainly be careful in these matters.

"Solitude. The commentary states: If one awakens to the principle of nature (*dharmatā*), one must not be separated from it for even a moment. If one is absent for even a moment, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) will manifest once again.
Therefore, one must exercise caution and apprehension as if standing on the brink of a deep abyss, preserving and entrusting oneself to the original nature so as not to fall into deviance.

The Way of Cultivating Solitude requires guarding against that which is hidden and subtle; when a tendency has just begun to sprout, or moves slightly before being fully manifested—whether it be good or evil—one must remain vigilant.
When thoughts seem to arise but have not yet arisen, one should immediately seize the moment to let them go and return to the fundamental principle; the merit of this is immense.
If one waits for good or evil thoughts to arise—until hatred and love, grasping and rejecting all erupt together—and only then attempts to subdue them, is that not far too late?

Therefore, the practice of being cautious when alone (*shendu*) is of the utmost importance. Thus it is said: "The gentleman nourishes the Way by being cautious when alone. [This applies to] joy and anger.
When sorrow and joy have not yet been manifested, it is called the Mean (*zhong*). When they are manifested and all accord with the proper measure, it is called Harmony (*he*).

The Mean is the great root of the world; Harmony is the pervasive path of the world. To bring the Mean and Harmony to perfection: therein heaven and earth find their station, and therein all things find their nourishment.
The commentary states: The Mean of the unmanifested is precisely true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*); quiescence and illumination are non-dual. It responds...

Things have no mind; it is also called innate knowledge (*liangzhi*). This may be called the fundamental substance of the Way. That which has been manifested as harmony is precisely wondrous wisdom (*miaohui*);

it can differentiate all phenomena while remaining non-abiding and unstained, which is termed innate capacity (*liangneng*). This is named the Way of Attainment (*dadao*). Innate knowledge and innate capacity both originate from the substance of nature.
This substance encompasses the great void and nurtures all existence; therefore, it is said that by bringing forth central harmony (*zhonghe*), "Heaven and Earth find their places."
"All things are nurtured therein.

The Confucian said, "Please grant me further clarification regarding innate knowledge (*liangzhi*) and innate capacity (*liangneng*. The Master replied, "The function of innate knowledge and that of discriminative cognition (*shizhi*) are vastly different.
Innate knowledge knows without the mind; discriminative cognition knows with thought. Innate knowledge knows good and knows evil."
The True Knower does not abide in good or evil; it is the conscious awareness that knows good and knows evil, yet abides within them. This true knowledge is like a mirror reflecting objects:
black and white, beauty and ugliness are distinguished of themselves, yet not even a trace of their reflection remains within the substance of the mirror.

Conscious awareness arises from these reflected images and falsely gives rise to discrimination, engaging in acceptance and rejection that obstructs one's own fundamental luminosity. Thus, one unites with sensory dust and turns one's back on awakening. Such is the nature of true knowledge and awareness.
One must discern for oneself; if there is a discrepancy as slight as a hair’s breadth, one is already a thousand li away from the truth. True capability is wisdom:
it can differentiate all phenomena, skillfully govern the worldly path, remain unstained by circumstances, and function with sovereign ease, such that every matter is without obstruction.
Question: "Confucius was 'empty and empty,' and Yan Hui was frequently 'empty. I do not know whether the principle of these two kinds of emptiness is the same or different. The Master said:

"Confucius’s 'empty and empty' means he was empty by means of emptiness, and empty by means of emptiness. This emptiness of emptiness is suchness; this suchness is true suchness; true suchness is one's original nature.
Yanzi studied to become a sage, yet he had not yet realized true suchness and could not avoid having thoughts. Although..."
When a thought arises and moves, it vanishes as soon as one is aware of it; this is what is meant by "returning before one has gone far. For this reason, the Sage Confucius praised Yanzi, saying:

"Hui is nearly there; he is frequently empty. When asked about this, the Master said: "The Way I teach is unified and runs through all things. I do not yet understand what this "one" is. The Master said: "The 'one' is precisely..."
Nature. Nature is principle; principle is the Way; the Way is oneness. Question:

“To overcome oneself and return to ritual propriety, and the whole world will come to possess benevolence. The Master said: “To overcome one’s own emotional consciousness and restore the heavenly principle.”

Ritual (*li*) is the regulation and refinement of principle (*li*). Benevolence (*ren*) is the virtue and function of the mind. When a person can overcome delusion and restore their true nature, the whole world will turn toward benevolence, as its essence is one.
Question: The Book of Documents says, "The human mind is perilous; the Dao-mind is subtle. Only through refinement and singleness may one truly hold fast to the Mean. Master [Shandao]:
It is said: The human mind arises and ceases without ceasing; therefore, it is perilous and lacks peace. The Dao-mind is empty, numinous, and serenely illuminating;
therefore, it is subtle and difficult to perceive. Purity constitutes the numinosity within emptiness, and oneness constitutes the emptiness within numinosity.

To hold this as a fixed formulation—that "the center" is the substance of nature—the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings are fundamentally rooted in this single principle. If one departs from the mind and nature, all such [teachings] are entirely demonic discourse.
Question: How does one study the Way of Yanzi—to not transfer anger and not repeat a mistake? The Master said: "Anger is movement; it is not mere resentment.
When Yanzi’s mind moved, he immediately released it and did not continue with a second thought; therefore, it is called 'not transferring.
His mind was always centered on one point, responding to affairs without partiality. When there was a mistake, he corrected it immediately; this is called 'not being dual.'"
Question: "The Sage washes his heart with the *I Ching* and withdraws to hide in the profound secrecy (*mi*). The Master said: "Washing the heart means purifying delusion;
withdrawing to hide means returning to the Real. When both the Real and delusion are simultaneously extinguished, it is therefore called 'secrecy' (*mi*)."
Question: "Without knowing or perceiving, one follows the pattern of the Emperor. The Master said: "True nature is like a mirror; it reflects objects without intention.

As soon as there is knowledge or perception, one falls into the realm of consciousness. Confucius said: "What do I have that can be known? I have no knowledge. Zen speaks of not knowing and not perceiving;
this is the very marrow of the Buddha-way.
Question: "The Master ate coarse grain and drank water; he rested his arm on it as a pillow, and yet joy was found therein.
I do not know what it was that he found joyful. The Teacher said: "Joy is true joy, not worldly pleasure. That which is found joyful is the principle of Heaven (tianli)."

That which is known is the mandate of Heaven (*ming*). One who delights in Heaven and knows its mandate has neither joy nor sorrow; their wondrous nature is luminously clear, and that joy is difficult to describe.
Question: Is the joy of Yanzi with his single bamboo bowl and gourd ladle the same as the joy of the Sage, Confucius? The Master said: "Yan Hui attained Confucius."
The Way is the joy of being without both elation and sorrow; its principle is fundamentally the same [as that of the sages].

Yan Duobao took this as his lifelong commitment. A questioner asked: "The workings of the High Heaven leave no sound and no scent. The Master said: "Emptiness is inherently without sound; the void is inherently without scent.
Although there is neither sound nor scent, the Way of Heaven is not obscured thereby."
Question: Zilu asked about death, and the Master replied, "While you do not yet know life, how can you know death?
What was the intended meaning of this response? Master: If you know the day, you will know the night; if you know the beginning, you will know the end.

If you first awaken to the appearance of that which precedes birth, you will then know the place where one establishes one’s life and rests at the very end. From where does life come? [And what of] death?
"Where does it return? From the beginning to the end, its root is one. Question:
"What is meant by the 'infant mind' (*zhizixin*)? The Master said: "The infant mind is pure, singular, and without delusion. The infant is not the Great Way itself;
we simply take the mind that is free from discrimination. It is like an adult who has attained thorough penetration and knows all phenomena, yet does not lose [that state]."
"The heart of an infant—this alone can be called the Way.
Question: "Yan Yuan was like one who is dull; Zhou Dunyi preserved his simplicity; Cheng Hao sat upright; and Li Zhongsu loved stillness.

If their conduct was such as this, what was the reason for it? The Master said: "This is the realization of principle and the cultivation of the Way; it is the path for transcending the mundane and entering the sacred. Hereafter...
The Confucians do not value the gate of awakening; they strive only for extensive learning and wide hearing, all of which come from the outside to supplement and stimulate [the mind].
They are unable to apply effort within the ground of the mind to bring forth true wisdom. What you have asked of these various schools may indeed be called "true learning."
Question: "Though I have studied much, I am unable to attain sudden enlightenment. I do not yet know what texts I should examine that might serve as a gateway for entering into the principle.

The Master said: "True investigation and genuine realization do not reside in words and letters. Even if one has studied extensively and mastered a vast array of books, there will be too many intellectual paths and too much analytical understanding;
these, in turn, will obstruct the original mind and become companions to consciousness. It is like a person counting another's treasures."
Since you do not possess even half a coin’s worth of [understanding], you must simply set aside all external studies and single-mindedly investigate the four endpoints.
Before any thought has arisen, what is your true face? Amidst movement and stillness, pursue this inquiry at every moment: what is the underlying principle?

Guard only this one thought-moment; harbor no second intention. Do not engage in deliberation, do not rely on intellectual understanding, do not wait for enlightenment, and do not seek conceptual realization.
This principle must not fall into the state of quiescent extinction, nor must it be lost in the realm of nothingness. One must only investigate deeply.
Before any thought has arisen, as days pass and months deepen, there comes a state of pure oneness without duality, where the thinking mind cannot reach and the conscious intellect cannot function.
When the time arrives, this principle will manifest of itself. Upon seeing forms or hearing sounds, it pierces through the nostrils; with a single "ha!"—a cold, piercing cry.
When the ash and beans burst forth, the mind-ground opens and the original nature is revealed. Thereafter, you may instruct students and guide the people;
even matters such as regulating the family and governing the state are none other than the wondrous functioning of your own mind-nature.

Question: Those of superior capacity attain sudden enlightenment and understand directly and clearly. For those of middling or inferior capacity whose habitual tendencies are heavy, how should they preserve and maintain [their realization]?

The Master said: After awakening to the principle, one should preserve and maintain it according to circumstances. One must be cautious, reverent, and alert, as if standing before a sovereign or one’s father. With utmost sincerity and true respect, the original nature will not be lost.
By preserving it in this way, after a long time, it will become natural.
Question: "Suppose one should lose mindfulness; what is to be done then? The Master said: "In the study of Yanzi, there is 'returning before one has gone far.
In a single moment, one spontaneously returns to the fundamental principle."
The Daoist Shi Daobian said, "Our teachings and those of Śākyamuni are very different. The Master asked, "In what way are they different?

Daobian said, "Śākyamuni’s teaching cultivates nature (*xing*) but does not cultivate life-force (*ming*); our teaching can cultivate both nature and life-force together. The Master asked, "What is nature? What is..."
This is the Way of Life (Ming). Dao said: "Those who cultivate Nature leave the palace to practice concentration; those who cultivate Life seek the Mysterious in the Water Palace. The Master asked:
"What is meant by 'leaving the palace to practice concentration'? What is meant by 'seeking the Mysterious in the Water Palace'? Dao replied: "Leaving the palace to practice concentration..."
"Concentrate the mind without movement to preserve the spirit; seek the mystery within the watery realm. Refine the essence into qi to solidify the physical form.

When both form and spirit are wondrous, one merges with the Dao in its true state. The Master said, "The teachings of Śākyamuni focus exclusively on cultivation and do not involve refining the essence and qi to solidify the form and preserve life."
You do not yet know that withdrawing from the palace to practice meditative concentration—wherein the mind and breath rely upon one another—is the dharma of the Two Vehicles.
Refining the essence within the water-palace, transforming qi to flow in reverse, and penetrating the gates to solidify the physical form are merely arts for prolonging life.

The supreme vehicle of the Buddha-dharma is the sudden awakening to the nature of the mind, wherein the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the myriad things, and one's own body and mind are all but illusory shadows within the nature; they have no inherent existence.
To rely on illusions to cultivate reflections—is this not an excessive error? An ancient worthy said: "The practitioners of the Way (xian) are attached to form and spirit and cannot relinquish them.
Furthermore, form and spirit are but deluded thoughts manifested within true nature; they are not reality.

One can only laugh at the Daoist teachings, for their eminent sages of past and present have failed to awaken to perfect enlightenment and have misunderstood the ultimate principle, falsely [taking what is unreal to be real].

The mind and breath relying upon each other is called the cultivation of nature (xing). Refining the essence (jing) to transform it into vital energy (qi) to solidify the physical form is called the cultivation of life (ming).
When both form and spirit attain a state of wondrous transcendence, they are far removed from the original nature.
Daoyun said: "The followers of the Yin-ghosts are unable to practice the dual cultivation; instead, they give rise to false slanders. My Way consists of the Two Vehicles;
you must clarify this for me, and only then will my mind be subdued. The Master said: "Those who study the Way of the Immortals arise from among sentient beings.

Although they know that birth and death are the ultimate suffering, they do not awaken to the Supreme One Vehicle. They remain deludedly attached to within the physical body, falsely seeking [the truth] within the fleshly heart."

There is a divine nature called "True Mercury," also known by the alternative name "The Virgin. Concentrating the spirit without movement, one practices meditative stabilization within the Palace of Separation.

The vital essence within the kidneys is called "True Lead," also known by the alternative name "The Infant. Refining the essence to transform it into energy, one seeks the Mystery within the Water Treasury.
The mind is "True Earth," also named "The Yellow Old Lady. According to the method of practicing meditative stabilization, one must necessarily...

To be exclusively devoted to seated meditation, employing the mind to regulate the breath and restraining the body from movement is called "subduing the tiger. To concentrate the spirit and harmonize the vital energy (*qi*) so that the mind is settled and unmoving is called "taming the dragon.
When body, mind, and intention are unified, it is called "returning to the earthen cauldron," remaining in a state of profound stillness and immobility.
For this reason, they cultivate the nature. Zhang Ziyang said: "The true soil captures the true lead; the true lead restrains the true mercury.

When lead and mercury return to the crucible of earth, body and mind are tranquil and unmoving. The Daoists recognize that this mind and breath rely upon one another, yet they falsely claim that the Buddhist teachings are partial in their cultivation.
How could they not be mistaken in their understanding of the supreme and ultimate principle? Little do they realize that every person inherently possesses the vast and great mind.

The nature (prakṛti) envelops the great void; it is neither existent nor non-existent, neither internal nor external, and is fundamentally unmoving. It requires no cultivation of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Yet, without cause, you take the illusory consciousness within the body and, using illusion to solidify illusion, call this "cultivating the nature. This is truly to mistake a thief for one's own son.
You claim that the true nature is inherently possessed and can be fully realized through cultivation, yet you do not depart from the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). If such power of concentration...
"Exhausted, one falls back into the lower realms.
Daoyun said, "To leave the palace to practice meditation—such a saying is like seeking the profound in the depths of the water. You must discern this. The Master said:

Seeking the profound within the Water-Palace, one guards and cherishes the vital essence (*jingqi*). Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, reflect back upon the interior of the navel at a depth of one inch and three-fifths;

this is called the Sea of Qi (*qihai*). Maintain it without attachment and illuminate it without dwelling. When body and mind have been settled for a long time, the *kan* and *li* trigrams unite and intersect.

The heart-fire descends; the kidney-water ascends. Essence becomes full and qi becomes rounded. The inner kidneys are like fire. At the end of Hai and the beginning of Zi, the qi moves at the Tailbone (Weilu).
Using the mind to inhale and lift it, it passes through the Central Channel (Zhongchong) and the Spine (Jiaji), straight up past the Jade Pillow (Yuzhen), reaching the Celestial Valley (Tiangu).

Furthermore, he transforms it into a golden liquid with a sweet and fragrant flavor. Swallowing it down through the nine palaces, it falls into the Yellow Court (Huangting), which is called "the cessation of the mingling of the dust of Heaven and Earth.
A single drop falls into the Yellow Court; from this point on, one becomes harmonious and refreshed, the four limbs feel light and agile, and the One Qi circulates throughout the body.
It nourishes the internal organs, restores the face to the appearance of youth, and extends one’s years for longevity. An ancient immortal’s verse says: “The Dharma-water can tide the secret pass;
In leisure, day and night, it dispels the cycle. If within this there is congestion, all manner of ailments arise;

As soon as it is unblocked and flows freely, the countenance is stabilized. The Immortal of Wu further said: “When the vital energy returns to the primordial sea, longevity is inexhaustible. This art is known as the Golden Elixir (Jin-ye).

Refining the physical form and practicing meditative concentration are the sovereign methods for preserving the spirit. When both body and spirit are wondrously perfected, one merges with the Dao in its true essence.
Once the merit is complete, according to the depth of one's blessings: those whose practice is vast ascend to the celestial palaces;

those whose merit is slight temporarily dwell on Mount Penglai or reside in a Cavernous Heaven (Dongtian) for three to five hundred years, or two to three thousand years, before returning once more to the human realm to accumulate further merit and cultivate their conduct. To nurture...

To cultivate merit and wisdom, the first principle is to practice the profound. When the Supreme Deity summons one, one follows the ranks to take one’s place; yet the ranks of the immortal officials are not uniform.
If one practices according to this [superficial method] while claiming it is identical to the Way of the Buddha, it is much like looking toward the Cao Gate from Zhengzhou—it is far, far removed.

Daowu said, "The practice of 'the mind and breath relying on each other' is the Dharma of the Two Vehicles. Why then did Bodhidharma come from the West and transmit the *Taisi Jing* (Sutra on Embryonic Respiration)?

The Master replied, "The Patriarch came from the West to transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal. How could he have intended for 'the mind and breath relying on each other' to be the Buddha’s Most Supreme Vehicle?

Before Bodhidharma had yet arrived in this eastern land, everyone here was already practicing *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight); why would they have needed to trouble themselves by traveling such a great distance?"
Furthermore, to transmit the practice of the embryo is to place a head upon a head; it may be called adding lips to a beak.

For this reason, those in China who are beginners in the study of the Way do not awaken to the nature of mind, but merely practice *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, as well as the four *dhyānas* and eight *samādhis*, yet they do not realize the Buddha-mind.
Therefore, our First Patriarch came by sea to point directly to the one mind and see one's nature to become a Buddha.

It is unknown who falsely fabricated the "fetal breath" (tāi-hsi) and falsely claimed the name of Bodhidharma, using the "separate transmission outside the teachings" to delude later generations, such that they could not distinguish between gold and brass.
Daowu said, "The method of *tāixī* (embryonic respiration) is spurious; it is not the Supreme Vehicle of the Buddha. What evidence is there for such a claim?

The Master replied, "The method of *tāixī* is like being in the mother’s womb: profound and obscure, with body and mind in perfect stillness. After a long time, meditative concentration is perfected."
The spirit and the vital energy (qi) bind together, refining them into an illusory form. The conscious spirit wanders abroad, traversing ten thousand li in an instant;
it roams at ease and with autonomy, yet it has no connection whatsoever with the One Vehicle of the Buddhas. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:

"Among those who practice and study, although they may presently achieve the nine successive meditative absorptions, they do not attain the exhaustion of outflows to become Arhats, all because they cling to these deluded thoughts of birth and death."
One mistakenly takes this as reality, yet fails to realize that within this illusory body there is fundamentally no life or nature.
My true life and nature do not reside within or without; they envelop the great void and are spontaneously perfected from the beginning, requiring no cultivation or realization.

Disciples of later generations who receive this teaching and awaken to this life and nature can manifest immeasurable wondrous bodies, deliver immeasurable sentient beings, and accomplish immeasurable adornments.

Yan: "He is capable of performing immeasurable Buddha-works. Yet, without cause, he recklessly takes the methods of *tai-xi* (embryonic breathing) and mistakenly identifies them as the purport of the 'separate transmission outside the teachings.
It is lamentable that his own eyesight is not clear; he deludes beginners and makes it difficult for them to discern. To take the small for the great—the error is no minor matter."

Dao-yun said: "Within body and mind, there is fundamentally no life-force (xing) or destiny (ming). The spirit within the present heart and the breath that comes and goes—these are not my true nature (zhenxing) or true destiny (zhenming).
By causing this spirit and breath to coalesce together and return to the pneuma-cavity (qixue), one forms the Great Elixir (Dadan).
Naturally, the body becomes light and the spirit wondrous; one is then able to travel through the eight extremities of the heavens."
A human being attains great mastery; this is called the dual cultivation of life and nature (*xing-ming*). It is the ultimate Great Way of the Immortals.
The Master said: "The spirit within the mind is delusion; the breath of respiration is an illusion. If one takes these illusions and delusions to be the true life and nature,"

Although they have thus cultivated and achieved such states that their spirits and bodies become light and subtle, enabling them to travel through space at the distance of ten thousand *li* in an instant and live for several million years,
they dwell deep within mountain caves and blessed lands to attain sainthood; yet, failing to awaken to perfect enlightenment, when their retribution is exhausted,
they return once more to be scattered among the various realms of existence.

Daoyun said, "In Buddhism, one cultivates nature. If one is biased toward the yin and lacks the yang, even if one attains cultivation and realizes the nature, one will instead become a clear and ethereal ghost.
The Master said, "Yin and yang, ghosts and spirits, are matters of the period after the empty kalpa (*śūnyakalpa*). The wondrously luminous true nature is the principle prior to the empty kalpa.
If one takes the principle prior to the empty kalpa and identifies it with the matters of the period after the empty kalpa, such a person..."
Not only do they fail to understand yin and yang, but their confusion and perversion are extreme.
The Way says: "In Buddhism, cultivation is biased toward yin; in our teaching, cultivation is balanced as yang. This is discussed throughout the alchemical scriptures and the *Zi-shu*.

This is not my own fabrication. The Master said: "In the Daoist practice of dual cultivation (*shuangxiu*), one mistakenly identifies the conscious spirit within the mind as the 'yin within yang,' and the vital essence and qi within the body as the 'yang within yin. By gathering the qi and unifying the spirit, the spirit becomes concentrated and the qi remains stable;
this is called 'taking the *kan* to fill the *li*. It is the process of transforming the yin within yang to achieve the robust body of *qian*, thereby refining it to completion."
The Golden Elixir: after ten months the embryo is formed, and for nine years it is nurtured. When it emerges from the crown of the head, it is called the Yang-Spirit (yang-shen).
When dispersed, it becomes wind; when gathered, it takes form. It travels throughout the world with ease and spontaneity. Through meritorious cultivation, it ascends to the celestial palaces.

With his merits being subtle, he lived in seclusion on Mount Penglai. If one relies solely on this [practice], yet does not cultivate samādhi, once the retribution of their immortality is exhausted, they will fall back down into the realm of ghosts.
As an ancient worthy’s verse says: "The student of the Way does not recognize the Real; it is only because from of old they have recognized the spirit.
For immeasurable kalpas, this has been the root of birth and death; the deluded person calls it the 'original person. This is the superior vehicle of the Buddha's teaching. See...

Its nature is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), profound and still like the great void. Its essence is identical to the *dharmadhātu*; it is neither yin nor yang, neither emerging nor entering. If pulled forward, there is no front;
if drawn back, there is no rear. If lifted up, there is no above; if pressed down, there is no below. It has been eternally luminous since antiquity and remains unobscured until now.
Although it possesses no form or appearance, it can manifest as both retribution and transformation bodies. How could it merely manifest a single body? It can transform into a thousand.
With ten billion bodies, he delivers sentient beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges and achieves the adornment of myriad virtues. Those of shallow capacity harbor doubts;
how could they believe and accept this?

Daoyun said, "In our teachings it is said: 'If one cultivates nature but does not cultivate life, the numinous spirit will find it difficult to enter the sacred state even after ten thousand kalpas. The Master said:
The principles of the study of life (*ming*) differ greatly. If one does not investigate them deeply, I fear it will mislead future students.

This mountain monk will not begrudge his speech as I shall distinguish these matters for you in minute detail. Regarding the two characters for "cultivating life" (*xiu-ming*), there is both principle (*li*) and vital energy (*qi*).

There are two meanings of the life of principle and two kinds of the life of energy. I shall first clarify the life of energy, and subsequently discuss the life of principle. First, as for the life of energy:

Solidify the root and open the gateway. Constantly sit in a state of partial stillness, reflecting back upon the qi-sea (*qihai*). Let the true intention remain undispersed; it shall be limpid and free from attachment.

As days pass and months deepen, the essence will fill and the qi will become complete. The inner kidneys will blaze like fire, urgently striking and vibrating. Regulate the breath through the nose until it is even and harmonious.

Urgently draw up the anal region and focus the mind to lead it upward; this is called "gathering the medicine. The Immortals say: "When the *gui* (the water element) arises, one must gather it immediately;
if one waits too long, it is unfit for tasting. Within half a moment, the vital essence surges upward, passing through the *weilu* (the coccyx) with a distinct, audible sound.

The breath passes through the center, traversing the spine and piercing straight through the *yùzhěn* (the occipital bone). Exert effort to transport it upward until it reaches the crown of the head (*dǐngmén*).

When the qi is about to descend, draw it in through the nose; it spontaneously transforms into sweet and fragrant nectar (*gānlù*), which is swallowed down through the nine palaces (*chónglóu*) and falls into the yellow chamber (*huángfáng*).

This is called "The Golden Crystal Flying from Behind the Elbow. It is also known as "Closing the Ren Vessel and Opening the Du Vessel. From this, the qi in the *dantian* becomes warm; spirit and qi become harmonious and surging;
the skin becomes moist and lustrous; it flows through the four limbs; the face returns to a youthful complexion; and one attains longevity and increased years.
Viewed from this perspective, even if the arts of prolonging life collectively grant a total lifespan of a thousand years, they ultimately end in decay and ruin.

Failing to awaken to the nature of the mind, one falls back into the various realms of existence. To claim that such arts can lead to the state of a sage is to delude future generations; it is truly a great deception.
Regarding the "life-force of the two qi": when the qi coagulates and returns to its root, while the person is in the mother’s womb, they follow the mother’s respiration.
Upon birth, once the umbilical cord is severed, a single point of ordinary qi settles in the *dantian*, where it dwells like a tortoise, inhaling and exhaling the primal qi.
In one day and one night, the coming and going of thirteen thousand five hundred breaths all leak out through the mouth and nose;
they cannot return to their source or revert to the qi-cavity. Therefore, life is not long and the physical body is not firm.

One must practice while walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, returning to the source to regularly replenish the Qi-sea. When the Qi abides, the form arises; when the spirit is concentrated, the Qi abides.
When spirit and Qi coalesce, it is called the Yang-spirit (yang-shen). After a long period, it emerges from the body to travel throughout the world, according to the depth of one's cultivation.
Ranks are not equal; when retribution is exhausted, one returns once more. Those who are born as humans in this world may again commit evil deeds and sink into the three miserable realms.

To claim that this Way brings liberation from saṃsāra is false speech. Without cultivating this Way, it is difficult to enter the ranks of the sages; one will surely be ridiculed by the wise. The Master said:
"The two studies of *qi* (vital energy) and *ming* (destiny) have been distinguished quite clearly. As for the two meanings of *li* (principle) and *ming*, I beg you to explain them further."

The Master said: "The two principles of 'principle' (li) and 'life-force' (ming) pertain to being entangled [in delusion] and being free from entanglement. When entangled, one takes emotion as life-force; when free from entanglement, one takes emptiness as life-force.

When entangled, movement constitutes the loss of life-force; the cessation of emotion constitutes the cultivation of life-force. When free from entanglement, merging with emptiness constitutes the ultimate life-force."
Furthermore, it is called "returning the mandate" (*fuming*). The Confucians call it the "Mandate of Heaven" (*tianming*); the Buddhists call it the "Dharmadhātu. This is the study of the Mahāyāna;
it may be termed the principle of the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*). Cultivating and realizing based upon this is called the "mandate of principle" (*liming*).
If one relies on the "mandate of vital energy" (*qiming*) without awakening to the mandate of principle, one will ultimately end in emptiness and will never attain the Great Way.
Daoist: The Immortal Master has said, "One who sees their nature does not know their destiny; where will they ultimately return?

I do not yet understand whether this knowing of destiny refers to principle (*li*) or vital energy (*qi*). Master: One who sees their nature knows the mandate of Heaven for themselves. As for the final step, it is to merge with the Void as one body. Confucian:
To exhaust principle and fully realize nature, thereby reaching the mandate of Heaven. Buddhist: That which is entangled in worldly existence is called the Tathāgata.

The *garbha* (womb-store), when emerging from the entanglements, is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*. If one refines the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and life-force, yet the spirit relies upon and becomes bound by that breath, taking it as its locus of selfhood, one will not escape the exhaustion of karmic retribution and will inevitably fall back into the various realms of existence.
One must know the mandate of destiny (*daivam*) before it can be called the fundamental principle.
Daowu said: "One Yin and one Yang are called the Correct Way. When Yang is solitary and Yin is scarce, the myriad things do not arise.

Why, then, do you speak of 'neither Yin nor Yang'? If there were no Yin and no Yang, how would that differ from inert emptiness? The Master said: "Movement constitutes Yang; stillness constitutes Yin.
The Two Polarities, the Four Images, the Five Elements, and the Eight Trigrams are all matters that occur after the differentiation of the Great Ultimate."
The Nature (xing) is the principle prior to the Great Ultimate (taiji). Within the Great Ultimate, even yin and yang have not yet been differentiated;
how much more so before the Non-Ultimate (wuji)? How could there be yin and yang? That which is inert emptiness is called "without spirit" (wuling); that which possesses spirit is not inert.

Later students do not realize this and falsely give rise to nihilistic views (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). The Buddhist says: "Suchness is unmoving; it is always clearly aware. The Confucian says: "It is silent and still..."
Movement. It is stirred and immediately becomes pervasive. The Way teaches that after body and mind have become unmoving, there further arises the infinite, true mechanism.
The three teachings instruct their disciples; their principles are no different. If one awakens to true emptiness, then it will be void yet spiritually lucid, never obscured.

The Daoist said, "In our Daoist teachings, one practices the dual cultivation (*shuangxiu*) and attains transcendence in a single lifetime. In the Buddhist teachings, one practices only partial cultivation;
thus, it cannot avoid the decay of the physical form. If one truly achieves the Way, that is well; otherwise, one must return again, inevitably undergoing the suffering of migration and rebirth.

The Master replied, "You see only the attainment of transcendence in a single lifetime, yet you do not know of the cultivation accumulated through successive kalpas. As for the Daoists, there were Ma Danyang and Qiu Changchun."
For three lifetimes they have been companions; for ten generations they have practiced cultivation. Upon first appearing in this world, they suddenly awaken to the True Path.

That you now see those of sharp faculties accomplishing their task in a single lifetime is entirely due to the accumulation of meritorious conduct over distant kalpas. It is because of this that they are able to manifest realization in the present life.
Do not cling to one-sided views, nor insist that realization must occur only in the present life.
Daoyun said, "The study of qi and the vital essence (jing) is false and not true. According to this teaching, would the arts of longevity not be useless?
The Master replied, "Refining the essence to transform it into qi, and the gathering of qi to give rise to form—these are the arts for cultivating the life-force to prolong one's years.

If one relies on these to achieve liberation, the harm done to people will not be slight. One must attain sudden enlightenment regarding the nature of the mind; only then can one transcend the mundane and enter the sacred."

Question: Regarding the elixirs of clay and water, and the wondrous arts of turning base metals into gold and silver, I do not yet understand their principle: are they heterodox or orthodox? The Master said: "Wealth, sex, fame, food, and sleep—these are the five roots of hell.
If the five desires are not vacated, birth and death will not cease. To study the Way authentically, one must sever affection and cut off love;

only by upholding the precepts and clarifying the mind can one realize the ultimate principle. To employ them perversely for no reason, seeking instead beautiful women, is to act contrary to the truth."
War involves harming others to benefit oneself; it not only greatly destroys one's innate goodness, but in days to come, one cannot escape the Fire Hell.
The Buddha said: "For sentient beings who indulge in lust, evil karma becomes ever deeper. The 'flower-retribution' consists of various illnesses, while the 'fruit-retribution' is the bed of fire.

Furthermore, there is a class of people with deluded karma who covet wealth and seek profit by burning reeds and refining mercury. When asked why they do this, they falsely claim, "I am practicing the Way," as was done in antiquity.
People abandon their greed for wealth and sink their treasures into the sea; yet now, they instead employ lead and tin to practice the Way.

Such a pursuit of the Path is truly preposterous and extraordinary. One can only lament those who crave wealth and lust after beauty, casting themselves onto the path of suffering and evil in the three realms of existence.
Dao said: "The Great Sage Laozi transformed the barbarians and became a Buddha. He did not realize that Śākyamuni was actually a disciple of Laozi.
The Master said: "The Buddha was born in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhao of the Zhou dynasty, the year Jiayin, and passed away in the fifty-third year of King Mu, the year Renshen.
He lived through the reigns of Kings Gong, Yi, Xiao, Yi, Li, Xuan, You, Ping, Huan, Zhuang, Xi, Hui, Xiang, Ding, Kuang, and [Jing]."
The *Ding* [dynasty] shared sixteen kings. Three hundred and forty-four years after its extinction, in the third year of King *Ding*, Laozi was born.
When he crossed the Flowing Sands, the Buddha-dharma spread far and wide throughout the five regions of India as well as neighboring countries.

It had already been more than three hundred years since the world heard of the Buddha’s True Dharma, yet they falsely fabricated the story that "Laozi transformed the Hu people and became a Buddha. This occurred during the Jin dynasty.
During the reign of Emperor Hui, Wang Fu falsely fabricated the "Deceiving the Sage" [text], which resulted in his own tongue being plucked out; how could his crimes be redeemed?
Dao Yun stated that in the third year of King Ding’s reign, the "Posterior Heaven Laozi" and the "Anterior Heaven Laozi" were born, and subsequently transformed the barbarians into Buddhas.
"It truly exists. The Master said: "Before the chaotic state was divided, when all was vast and formless, there was the primordial vital energy; this is called the 'pre-heaven' (prior to the cosmos).

Once the Great Ultimate (Taiji) had split and heaven and earth began to separate, the myriad things came into being; this is called the 'post-heaven' (after the cosmos). The pre-heaven has no form; it is only in the post-heaven that images appear.
Since the Buddha’s birth during the reign of King Zhao is separated from that time by a vast distance, how could he have been of the pre-heaven?"

The formless nature of this [teaching] and the subsequent manifestation of its transformative influence after heaven constitute the true words regarding the groundless state; those who hear them cannot help but cover their noses.
Question: In our teaching, the cultivation of qi and life-force is an external art, and the mutual dependence of mind and breath belongs to the Two Vehicles. Is there still a Mahāyāna to be found?
"What is the principle for practicing it? The Master said, "There is a principle that can be practiced. He asked, "Please show me the principle that can be practiced.
The Master said, "The *Daodejing* and the *Qingjingjing*; practice according to these two scriptures and you will not err."

Question: "How many different names are there? Later students have misunderstood them. I beg the Master’s compassion to clarify them for easy understanding. The Master said: "If you have doubts, come and ask;
I shall not begrudge you my instruction. Question: "How do you explain the passage: 'The valley-spirit does not die; this is called the Mysterious Female'?

The Master said: "'Valley' means emptiness; 'spirit' means numinous awareness. That which is empty and numinous, yet never obscured, is called 'not dying. As for the 'Mysterious Female,' it is precisely this numinous awareness."
"Mechanism. As for the "spiritual mechanism," it is the true mind. Question: "What is the 'one aperture of the mysterious pass'? The Master said:

"When thought has not yet arisen and the mechanism has not yet sprouted, this is called the 'mysterious pass. That which is numinous within emptiness and wondrous within stillness is called the 'one aperture.

Question: "How is it that one 'takes from the Kan and fills the Li'? The Master said: "To eliminate delusion is to take from the Kan; to return to the mind is to fill the Li. Question: "How is it that one 'extracts...'"?
"Adding mercury to lead. The Master said: "To obliterate emotional attachments is to extract the lead; to empty the mind is to add the mercury. "How is it called 'establishing the furnace'?
The Master said: "It is neither within nor without. "How is it called 'setting up the cauldron'? The Master said: "It is not identical to the mind."

[Question: It is not separate from the mind. How can it be called the Golden Elixir (*jindan*)? [Master: It is perfectly round, eternally luminous since antiquity; it is brilliantly radiant, never obscured until this day. [Question:
How can it be called the Original Essence (*yuanjing*)? [Master: It is the wondrously luminous true essence, manifesting through the six faculties.
[Question: How can it be called the Original Vitality (*yuanqi*)? [Master: When the single mind is free from delusion, its virtuous energy nourishes the body. [Question: How can it be called...

[Question: "This is the primal spirit (*yuánshén*). The Master said: 'Its concealment and manifestation are unfathomable; its application is without fixed direction. How can this be called the 'fire-sign' (*huǒhòu')?

[Master] said: "A single thought is ten thousand years; ten thousand years are a single thought. [Question: "How can this be called 'warming and nourishing' (*wēnyǎng')? [Master] said: "Reflecting back to investigate the mind, neither becoming dull nor scattered.
[Question: "How can this be called 'subduing the dragon' (*jiànglóng')? [Master] said: "When the arising of the mind does not continue, it is metaphorically called 'subduing'."
"Dragon," [he asked]. "How is it called 'subduing the tiger'? The Master said, "To obliterate emotion and restore the nature; this is another name for subduing the tiger.

"How is it called 'movement and stillness'? The Master said, "Non-thought yet thought; thought yet non-thought. "How is it called 'water and fire'? The Master said, "The water of concentration and the fire of wisdom;
they are equal in learning and non-dual. "How is it called 'the true seed'? The Master said, "The spirit that responds to things."
[Question: "The spiritual capacity (*qi*) is the true seed. How can it be called 'pure yang'? [Master: "When not a single thought arises, the myriad conditions are empty and still.
[Question: "How can it be called 'pure yin'? [Master: "When the deluded mind is inverted, birth and cessation ceaselessly continue.
[Question: "What is meant by 'bathing'? [Master: "To purify the mind and release all burdens is called bathing. [Question: "What is meant by 'shedding the embryo'? [Master:]...
[The student] asked: "The numinous light shines alone, utterly transcending the sense organs and their objects. How can this be called 'returning to emptiness'? The Master said:

"When both person and phenomena are simultaneously extinguished, things and self become one. How can this be called 'attaining final realization'? The Master said: "It is the True Suchness that has emerged from the entanglements; it is the Pure Dharma-realm."
Question: For a beginner entering the gate, where does one begin? The Master said: First realize, then cultivate. Question: What is meant by "first realizing"? The Master said:
Take all habitual notions of subject and object, as well as all views of good and evil, and cast them outside your belly.

Do not dwell on any single point; instead, single-mindedly investigate the mysterious pivot: "Where does it lie? Throughout the two-and-six hours of the day and night, deeply probe this doubt and investigation. This is the one pivotal barrier.
The aperture—what kind of face and eyes does it have? When true doubt manifests before you, body and mind become one void; there remains only the single thought of investigation.

Once more, shatter that single thought, and the true nature will shine forth clearly; the Mysterious Barrier (xuān guān) appears. Thereafter, maintain this state in accordance with conditions, purifying away even the subtlest flow [of consciousness].
Only when you naturally attain oneness with the empty substance will you have reached final completion from beginning to end.

Question: Those of superior faculties attain sudden enlightenment and understand directly and clearly. However, for those of middling or inferior capacities, their past habitual tendencies are too heavy;

even if they attain sudden enlightenment, they cannot realize it suddenly. What expedient means are there to allow them to further nurture and preserve this state? The Master said: For one who has realized the principle, they should maintain it according to conditions (*yuan*).
Throughout the twelve hours of the day, amidst movement and stillness, do not dwell on existence externally, nor guard against emptiness internally. One—
Cultivate equanimity; let all things subside into stillness of their own accord. Should a thought suddenly arise, do not allow subsequent thoughts to follow.
As the ancient immortals said: "Once the spirit departs, immediately summon it back. When the spirit returns to the body, the vital energy naturally flows back.
If one practices thus morning and evening, the spiritual embryo of the infant will naturally form. This "spiritual embryo of the infant" is not a physical fetus; it is like the mind of an infant.
It is pure and simple, without external thoughts. A question was asked:
"Can maintaining the mind of an infant be called the Way? The Master said: "The infant's mind is not the Way; it is simply the state of being free from discrimination.
If you realize the infant's mind, do not cling to the infant's mind; you must further shift your position before you can attain greatness."

Fang asked, "What is meant by the 'Great Dharma'? The Master said, "When still, it is like the spirit of the valley; when moving, it is like drifting clouds. Its unfolding and rolling up leave no trace;
its appearing and disappearing leave no path. It does not wear precious garments, but temporarily dons soiled clothes. It walks upon what is not the Way, yet accomplishes the ultimate."

The Way: teaching and transforming according to the capacities of beings to universally deliver all sentient creatures. Only when one’s own merit and wisdom are both perfected does one realize the Great Enlightenment of the Golden Immortal.
*Record of Myriad Dharmas Returning to the Mind*, Volume One.
Record of the Ten Thousand Dharmas Returning to the Mind, Volume Two:

Sudden Enlightenment, Cultivation, and Realization. A monk asked: "What constitutes the fundamental principle (zong)? The Master said: "The ten thousand dharmas return to the principle; the principle is precisely the mind. This mind is empty and numinous."
It is pervasive and vast, non-abiding and unconditioned, without cultivation and without realization. As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha’s words take the mind as their essence;

having no gate is the Dharma-gate. From India to China, from antiquity to the present day, it has been handed down hand-to-hand by every Buddha and transmitted from master to master by every Patriarch.
This single mind alone is established as the fundamental essence of the school. This essence is pure, inherently perfect and luminous;

it is unstained when following the current, yet not impure when returning against the current. It does not diminish among ordinary beings, nor does it increase among sages. Although their conditions differ, this mind remains non-dual.

When wisdom realizes it, the radiance becomes manifest; when afflictions shroud it, the wondrous essence remains hidden. To cultivate apart from this is ultimately to become a follower of Māra or a heterodox teacher.
Question: What constitutes the teaching? The Master said: The Buddhas expounded the Dharma by provisionally opening up the three vehicles and five natures. The Bodhisattvas composed...
This treatise elucidates that the myriad dharmas are but the one mind. Through these explanations, later students may grasp the essential meaning, sever delusions, and return to the truth;
beginners may obtain the hare while forgetting the trap, and further cultivate themselves to realize the principle.

Question: Regarding the two gates of *zong* (principle) and *jiao* (teaching), are their principles the same or different? The Master said: "The *zong* is precisely the teaching without words; the *jiao* is precisely the *zong* with words. Question:

Since the principles of the two gates of *zong* and *jiao* are fundamentally one, why is it further said that there is a "separate transmission outside the teaching"? The Master said: "The teaching..."
It is only through language and written characters that one can skillfully understand; yet the essence transcends language and written characters, allowing for the sudden realization of the One Mind.
Therefore, it is called "the separate transmission outside the teachings," and also termed "the supreme principle."

The monk said, "In such a transmission of words, there is still depth and shallowness. The Master said, "Shallowness and depth depend on the person; the principle is fundamentally non-dual. The monk asked, "What is this non-dual principle?
The Master said, "Having heard the teachings and understood the principle, one must further apply cultivation and realization. One naturally accords with the Great Way of non-action (*wuwei*).
In the School of the Patriarchs, sudden awakening necessarily relies upon perfect cultivation before the fundamental mind of tranquil illumination can be restored."
Question: The Sūtra says, “The source of returning is non-dual; the expedient means have many gates. I do not yet know which gate allows for direct realization and liberation.

The Master said, “As for the two causes—the external and the internal—it is possible to realize them directly. The monk asked, “I request the Master to show me directly what these two causes, the external and the internal, are.
The Master said, “The external cause requires that one sever lust, killing, and stealing; the internal cause requires that one clarify the mind and see its nature. Question: For what reason?
Regarding the external causes, one must sever lust, killing, and theft. The Master said: "Sentient beings are entangled in birth and death because of thoughts of lustful desire;

they undergo the cycle of rebirth because of killing, which leads to the mutual repayment of life-debts; and they must return again because of theft, for which one must repay both principal and interest.

If these three types of causes are eliminated, the remaining physical substrate will be forever severed and no longer continue. Question: How does one clarify the mind and perceive the nature through internal causes? The Master said:
[The Master] said: "The mind is fundamentally pure; the nature is fundamentally empty. [The Questioner] asked: "How is it that the mind is fundamentally pure? The Master said:
"This mind is not the lump of flesh and blood within the physical body. Nor is this mind the deluded mind of arising and ceasing within the 'inch-square' of the heart.
Rather, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm, penetrating through the ten directions, transcending all dualities, and cutting off all conceptual play."

The Treatise states: It is neither extinguished nor born; it is neither existent nor non-existent. It is empty yet luminous, never obscured; perfect and wondrous, it responds to all things. Its unfolding and rolling up are unimpeded;
its appearing and disappearing are free and pervasive. Following conditions without changing, it is the eternally abiding true mind.
Therefore, the Buddhas of the past have universally realized this mind; the Bodhisattvas of the present study this mind together; and the late learners of the future shall all clarify this mind.
Sentient beings are deluded because they are deluded regarding this mind; practitioners attain awakening because they awaken to this mind. The entire Great Canon of Teachings reveals only this mind;
Bodhidharma came from the West to point directly to this mind; and the masters of past and present have revealed and instructed others regarding this mind.
This spirit is subtle and wondrous; it is difficult to describe in its entirety. I shall briefly cite one or two points so that future generations may believe and awaken.
Question: What is meant by "seeing that the nature is fundamentally empty"? The Master said: The self-nature of True Suchness is fundamentally empty and still.

It has no form and no marks; it is as profound and vast as empty space. It neither moves nor shakes; it remains eternally constant and immovable. This is called the "original face. It is also called "the positionless."
True Person: All mountains, rivers, and the great earth; grasses, trees, and groves; the myriad phenomena of the manifest universe;
and all dharmas, whether defiled or pure—each and every one flows forth from within this.
Question: Are the true mind and the original nature one or two? The Master said: "Neither one nor two. Question: Why are they not one? Why are they not two? The Master said:
"The original nature is the essence; the true mind is the function. The original nature is like a mirror; the true mind is like its light.
The light does not depart from the mirror, and the mirror does not depart from the light. As an ancient worthy said: "The nature is both luminous and wondrous; it is still and..."
Yet it is profoundly still, like the substance of a mirror. The mind then arises from this wondrous stillness as luminosity; it is perfectly integrated and illuminating, like the light of the mirror.
Because the light and the mirror are distinguished, they are not one; because the light and the mirror are fundamentally one, they are not two.

Question: Since it is said that the nature and substance of the Buddha and sentient beings are one and the same, why does the Buddha dwell in the realm of the sages while sentient beings remain in the state of the ordinary?

The Master said: The fundamental substance of the nature of both Buddhas and sentient beings is originally empty; it is because the mind has defilement and purity that they are designated as "sage" and "ordinary. Question:
"How is it that the mind has both defilement and purity? The Master said: "The fundamental nature is like a mirror—perfectly bright, empty, and still.

The true mind is like its light, illuminating objects without obscuration. When the sages respond to affairs without a [discursive] mind, coming and going without defilement, this is called pure light.

When sentient beings respond to affairs with a [discursive] mind, making distinctions between grasping and rejecting, this is called defiled light. Although defilement and purity differ, their substance is non-dual."
A monk asked, "Regarding the fundamental substance of the mind-nature, can it have limitations? The Master said, "It has. The monk asked, "How large is its substance?
The Master said, "It encompasses the ten voids and pervades all myriad existences. The monk said, "If the mind-nature is thus boundless and vast, why does it reside within the physical body?
The Master said, "Since beginningless time, all sentient beings have been imprisoned within the womb-cage."
The physical body is shackled by fetters, and deluded attachments are made firm. The vast nature of mind remains obscured within the body;

mistaking a thief for one’s own son, one is as if trapped in a great prison—when will one ever be able to escape? Not only are humans and devas deluded regarding this, but even those of the Lesser Vehicle remain likewise.

The monk said, "The nature of mind does not reside within the body. Who is it that is now able to think? The Master replied, "What you doubt and inquire about is the illusory consciousness within the body;
you take this capacity for thought and deliberation to be your 'mind. This is merely the reflected shadow of the six sense objects, which deludes your true nature.
Without cause, you stubbornly cling to it as being within, making it difficult to escape the prison of the womb. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says, the Buddha told Ānanda:
These are the delusive appearances of false thoughts regarding external objects that confuse your true nature.
From beginningless time until this present life, you have mistaken a thief for your own son, thereby losing your original constancy and undergoing the cycle of rebirth.

If you can attain clear understanding at this point, you will know that the mind of discursive thought is like a reflection in a mirror or flowers in the sky—manifesting as empty forms, yet fundamentally lacking any substantial reality.
The monk said, "Internal thoughts and the shadows of conditions from the six sense-objects—how can these be my wondrously luminous mind-nature?
The Master said, "Sentient beings do not realize that the vast mind-nature exists neither within nor without; instead, they mistake the shadows of sensory objects for reality.

They falsely imagine that empty space encloses the physical body, the physical body encloses the physical heart, and the physical heart encloses the true nature. Thus, they are bound layer upon layer, stubbornly clinging to greed."

[The disciple] says, "I love [this body]," yet fails to realize that the void, the great earth, the myriad things, and one's own body and mind are all illusory reflections manifested by my wondrously luminous mind-nature.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "When the gathering of conditions causes internal agitation and the pursuit of externals leads to wild flight, one takes this state of confused turmoil to be the mind-nature.
Once deluded and taking this as the mind, one is certain to be confused about it being within the physical body, not realizing that it exists outside the physical body."
As for the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind. Fearing that you have not yet awakened to this, I shall provide a metaphor:
the fundamental nature is like a vast mirror encompassing the entire Dharma-realm; the wondrously true mind’s spiritual illumination is like the radiance within the mirror;
and the mountains, rivers, the great earth, the myriad phenomena, and even the physical body and the conscious mind, are all entirely within the mirror.

This is the shadow within [the mirror]. Sentient beings mistake the shadow for reality, wallowing and drowning in the four modes of birth and the nine realms of existence. If one were to recognize the mirror, the true mind would naturally and instantaneously be restored.

Question: The nature of the mind is vast and great, encompassing and nurturing all things. It does not reside within the body; yet if one imagines it to be outside the body, it would merely envelop the flesh.
"Is this principle correct or not? The Master said, "No. The monk said, "If it is not within, it cannot be; if it is not without, it is not that.

This principle is deeply perplexing; I pray the Master resolve it for me. The Master said, "The fundamental nature is empty and pervasive; it is neither inside the body nor outside the body. The true mind has no fixed abode;
it is neither identical to the body nor separate from the body. Therefore, Ānanda clung to delusion without basis and was bewildered in the seven locations."
However, the Second Patriarch realized that there is no birth; with a single word, he accorded with the Way. If you are dull-witted, I shall provide another analogy for you:
the fundamental nature is like the vast ocean’s still water, and the true mind is like the light within that still water. Stirred by the wind of external objects, bubbles suddenly arise.
These bubbles are the physical body; the seawater is the Dharma-body. The moisture of the bubbles is the nature of consciousness; the moisture of the seawater is...

This is the original nature. The moisture of a floating bubble and the moisture of the ocean water are both moistures; their moist nature is fundamentally one, and thus they are neither internal nor external.
The moisture of the ocean water and the moisture of a floating bubble each possess their own singular moisture, which appears as if there were an internal and an external.

Ordinary beings, deluded and attached to the floating bubble, conversely abandon the boundless great ocean. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like abandoning the clear, vast oceans numbering hundreds of thousands, and instead recognizing only one [bubble]."
The substance of a floating bubble is designated as the entire tide, exhausting the vastness of the ocean. You all are, therefore, people who are doubly deluded.

If later students were to awaken to the fact that the moisture-nature of the bubble-water and the seawater are fundamentally one, how could there be any fixed attachment to distinctions such as "inner" and "outer"?
That one fails to attain this fundamental nature is truly lamentable.
The monk said: "The moisture of the ocean water is a metaphor for the nature of the Dharma-realm; the moisture of the floating bubbles is a metaphor for the consciousness within the body.

The nature of this moisture is non-dual, being neither internal nor external. Since it is neither internal nor external, when retribution is exhausted and life ends, one leaves this life and is born elsewhere; thus there is the appearance of entering and exiting."

"There is only coming and going. Why do you say there is no entering? The Master said, "If you cannot attain awakening through the instructions given above, yet instead seek the arising and ceasing of empty flowers, you may be called utterly ignorant.
This is all because from the very beginning you did not maintain your own nature; with a single thought of deluded movement, you became bound within the prison of the womb.
Life after life you have stubbornly clung to it as being definitely within the body, [claiming] there is exiting and entering, and coming and going."
There is going and coming; internal and external coming and going are like flowers in the sky. Although the flowers arise and perish, the sky is fundamentally unmoving.
Consciousness seems to enter and exit, but its nature is fundamentally unmoving. Just as flowers in the sky are illusory, the consciousness within the body is delusory.

Now, by using the illusion of flowers in the sky to clarify the delusion of bodily consciousness, their principle is non-dual. You must examine this for yourself. If you do not awaken to it, [you will remain lost].

Again, citing a scriptural analogy, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Suppose there is a person who takes a *piṅgala* bird-shaped bottle, plugs its two openings, fills it with empty space, and carries it a thousand li away to present as a gift to another country.
You should know that the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) is exactly like this, Ānanda. This empty space does not come from that place, nor does it enter here. Thus, Ānanda, if that..."

If it were to come from another direction, then since the space has already been displaced by the jar being placed inside, there should be a corresponding void in the location where the jar originally stood.

Furthermore, if it were to enter from this side, one should see the space emerge when the jar is opened and turned upside down. Therefore, one should know that the aggregate of consciousness (vijñānaskandha) is false and illusory;

it is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of a spontaneous nature. Commentary: "The *piṅgala* bird-jar" is the name for a type of jar. Blocking both its holes serves as a metaphor.

Regarding good and evil karma: the analogy of the jar represents the power of karma, which is able to lead consciousness to move. The space within the jar represents the consciousness that follows karma.
Although this space within the jar appears to have an "inside" and the space outside the jar appears to have an "outside," space has no dual nature; inside and outside are fundamentally one.
Therefore, it is neither internal nor external. The emptiness within a jar serves as a metaphor for the fundamental emptiness of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Because it is drawn by the karma of good and evil, consciousness wanders, just like one carrying a jar traveling a thousand li to another country to offer its contents; this illustrates the relinquishing of this life and receiving that one. As the Sūtra says:
"Ānanda, this empty space does not come from that direction, nor does it enter from this direction. This is a metaphor for casting off the body, just as [the space] leaves that direction.
Come! Yet the consciousness of the previous body has never diminished; it enters only when the body is thus received. And the consciousness of the subsequent body has never arrived from elsewhere.
