One should know that when the body dies, it does not go anywhere; before death, it was fundamentally not restricted to this place. When a body is born, it does not come from elsewhere;
before birth, it was likewise fundamentally pervasive throughout this place. The deluded do not understand this, and thus they claim it exists within.
There is coming and going. One who has attained awakening clearly realizes that the fundamental substance is originally devoid of "this" and "that";

how could there be coming and going? The monk said, "One who has attained awakening clearly realizes that the fundamental substance is originally devoid of coming and going, yet now we die here and are born there;

thus, there are still the appearances of going and coming. The Master said, "They arise when conditions assemble and perish when conditions end. Although they manifest the appearances of coming and going, they are perfectly luminous."

It is fundamentally unmoving; yet the diseased eyes of ordinary beings falsely perceive it as floating flowers in the sky, subject to birth and extinction, flowing and turning according to conditions.
As the Buddhist sutras state: "Good son, all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been subject to various inversions, like a person who has lost their way and mistakes the directions.
They falsely take the four great elements to be the characteristics of their own bodies, and they take the shadowy reflections of the six sense objects to be their own selves."
The characteristic of the mind is like that of a person with diseased eyes who sees flowers in the sky, even as numerous empty flowers vanish into space;

one cannot say there is a fixed place where they are extinguished. Why? Because there is no place of birth. All sentient beings, within this state of non-birth, delusively perceive birth and extinction;
this is what is called transmigrating through birth and death. Those of later learning who achieve sudden awakening realize that consciousness is an illusion.

While birth and cessation arise, the essence of the Perfect Enlightenment Mind remains eternally abiding and unmoving. As the Patriarch said: "Though the hundred members may decay and scatter, one thing remains forever numinous.
If you understand this mind, who is there to undergo birth and death?
The monk said, "Your exposition is most clear; there is nothing that is not fully understood. Why, then, did my body and mind first come to exist?

The Master said, "The true source is profoundly still, and the ocean of awakening is transparently pure. Originally, there was no trace of subject or object; how could there be any vestige of names or forms?

At the very beginning, there was non-awakening, and suddenly a moving mind arose. Because of this clarity, a reflecting consciousness was established; following that reflection, objective dust was established—the perceived division."

Suddenly it arises; its appearance is named "peaceful array. Like reflections appearing in a mirror, the sense-faculties and the physical body arise all at once. Next, the world-systems differ according to one's perceptions.
Finally, through attachment and aversion, the fruits of karmic continuity unfold. From this point on, they lose sight of the truth and sink into the three realms.
They undergo saṃsāra in vain, without any rest.
The monk said, "Truly as the Master says: at first there was no awareness, then suddenly a moving mind arose, and the root-body (indriya-kāya) was abruptly produced.

When the retribution of this illusory form is exhausted and the four great elements disperse, how does the illusory consciousness within the body enter a womb? The Master said, "In the daily activities of ordinary people..."
Driven by emotional attachments and karmic actions—whether virtuous or non-virtuous—one experiences results corresponding to their causes. At the moment of death, the great earth becomes dark;

yet wherever there is a karmic connection, a single point of luminous color appears. One rushes toward it and sees one’s parents in sexual union, giving rise to thoughts of either aversion or attachment.

Focus the mind and project [the consciousness] into it. The two drops, red and white, are held together in an instant like iron attracted by a magnet; they remain thus during the five stages of gestation.
Within the first seven days, it is called "impure mixture" (*kalala*); the father’s semen and the mother’s blood lie together like thin curd, and their blending is termed "mixture."
Impurity is called filth. Within the second week, it is called a scab; its shape is like that of a pea. It has the form of a scab.

The exterior and interior are like curd because blood has not yet been produced. Within the first twenty-one days, it is called "coagulation" (kalala); its form gradually coagulates as it approaches the state of blood.
Within the second twenty-one days, it is called "thickening" (arbuda); it gradually becomes firm and solid, and the five viscera begin to develop.
The period within the fifth seven-day interval is called the stage of form (*ākṛti-avasthā*). Blown by the internal winds, the various sense organs and physical forms are produced;

because the distinctions of the body and its four limbs arise, at the conclusion of the fifth seven-day interval, the five sense faculties are all complete. Within the sixth seven-day interval, it is called the stage of hair, nails, and teeth.
Within seven weeks, it is said to possess its faculties; all the internal organs and the five sense-faculties become complete. At the end of ten months, it emerges from the womb as a human being.
The consciousness-essence within the embryonic membrane divides into six functions: seeing, hearing, knowing, and perceiving, which then create karma according to their respective objects.
Life and death, death and life—the cycle of saṃsāra continues without rest.
A question was asked: "Does the consciousness that enters the womb have a form? The Master said: "It does. The questioner asked: "What is its form? The Master said:
The consciousness that enters the womb is called the intermediate state (*antarābhava*). Why is it called the intermediate state? It exists between death and birth;
as a human being, it possesses a body within this interval that corresponds to its future form of existence. Its stature does not exceed three feet.

They are about the size of a child aged five or six. Within the animal realm, their forms resemble those of animals; the same applies to other destinies, each appearing according to the state of rebirth.

Although their conscious form is small, they are capable of performing various karmic actions. They enter the womb by the side of the parents, giving rise to perverted thoughts of hatred and attachment.
In common worldly parlance, they are generally called "ghosts" (*guihun*).
The monk asked, "In this world, how is it that there are those who can seize an empty dwelling without entering a womb?

The Master said, "In this world, there are practitioners of the Way, or perhaps people of great merit, who do not enter a womb; rather, they wait for a place where conditions are favorable, and as soon as they emerge from their mother's birth."
With a single sound of [囗@力], a spark of numinous consciousness directly enters through the fontanelle. The fetal consciousness is driven away, and it seizes the empty dwelling to become a person.
This is an inconceivable realm; it is not something that can be achieved through intentional effort or contrivance.

The monk said, "As for the matter of worldly sentient beings whose retribution is exhausted and their lives have ended, who then cast themselves upon their parents, or perhaps undergo the experience of entering another body to suffer the punishments of hell—these things are likely not actually real. The Master said, "Hell is not non-existent; it exists because of the mind."
All sentient beings, through the karma of the ten habitual bonds, form these habits as causes; following their karma, they receive retribution, and their own minds manifest as hell.
There is no external realm whatsoever. As a verse in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "One should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: all things are created solely by the mind.
Thus, one knows that the suffering endured in hell is a manifestation of one's own mind. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Ānanda, these are called the ten causes of hell."

The six realms of retribution are all created by the deluded ignorance of sentient beings. Students of later generations must be careful not to hear that these hells are illusory and thereby become negligent, failing to sever their evil karma.
If they continue to indulge in such habits and follow their karma, the hells of their own minds will suddenly manifest before them;
if they then wish to escape, will it not be difficult? It is like a person living in this world who acts—
Good and evil deeds are of varying magnitudes, great or small; one receives their fruits according to the causes. When good is great, one’s own mind causes rebirth in heaven;
when evil is profound, one’s own mind causes a fall into hell. When good and evil are equal, one is born as a human or an animal.

When both merit and transgression are inferior, one does not immediately receive birth, but suddenly takes form; this is called the *antarābhava* body. Arising from nothingness in an instant, it is termed a "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*).
They are born naked, three feet in height, with all six sense-faculties fully sharp. Their coming and going is swift and unhindered; to others, they appear as mere shadows.
They die and are reborn within seven days; those of long life do not exceed seven times seven days, while those of short life are reborn after one, two, three, or seven days.
In common parlance, they are called "souls" (hún).
Question: “The fundamental nature is vast and expansive; its substance encompasses the great void. The true mind has no fixed abode and resides neither within nor without.

Yet, the consciousness-mind within the body is imprisoned in the womb-like prison. Does the true mind exist within this consciousness-mind, or must one seek the true mind apart from the consciousness-mind?
The Master said: “Gold exists within the ore; water exists within the waves. Thus it is with the *ālaya-vijñāna* when it is enmeshed in bondage—it remains hidden.”
It obscures True Suchness. Beginners must realize the distinction between the true and the false: by relying on the true mind, one swiftly realizes Bodhi;
by following the deluded mind, one drifts through birth and death.
The monk asked, "I do not yet understand: within the body, what is called the true consciousness and what is called the deluded consciousness?

The Master said, "True consciousness is numinous awareness; it takes still illumination as its essence. Deluded consciousness possesses cognition; it takes攀缘 (pān-yuán, grasping at conditions) as its essence.

The monk asked, "In what sense does deluded consciousness possess cognition and take grasping at conditions as its essence? The Master said, "Deluded consciousness is fundamentally empty. Because of the subject-object duality (*neng-sou*), it follows after objects and becomes divided."

It is distinct. Through hatred and attachment, one grasps and pulls; from moment to moment there is攀緣 (pān-yuán, clinging to objects), and from thought to thought there is chaotic ideation. One seizes upon sensory objects without ceasing and dwells in conceptualization without rest.
Between heaven and hell, one revolves through the various realms of existence. Not recognizing birth as birth, one recognizes death as death.
Like a monkey playing in a tree, or like a horse let loose in the countryside, one drifts and wanders through the three realms without a day of respite.
Question: "The deluded mind possesses cognition; what makes it illusory? The Master said: "The deluded mind is like the moon in water;

its cognition is like flowers in the sky. It arises from the subject-object duality and exists because of discrimination. It gives rise to the functioning of consciousness through the floating sense organs, forming the deluded cognition that confronts objects.

If separated from external phenomena, this mind has no substance. Because it arises as an illumination dependent on objects, when the objects perish, the illumination vanishes, and it is produced in accordance with thought."

Dust: when one contemplates emptiness, the dust subsides. If one were to take this reflected image as the true body of the Buddha, it could be called a cause of delusion and would result in the fruit of annihilation. How could such a phantom ever be real?

Question: How is it that the true mind is called spiritual awareness? Why is it said that it takes stillness and illumination as its essence? The Master said: "The true mind is profoundly serene. Its illumination does not arise from external objects;

it contains the void and accords with conditions, never engaging in deliberate effort. It is luminous and never obscured, clearly and constantly aware. When extended, it leaves no trace; when withdrawn, it leaves no mark.
It is like a clear pool reflecting the wilds, or like a bright mirror suspended in space, wherein the myriad phenomena are densely arrayed."
Suddenly, there is a vast and empty discernment: neither emerging nor entering, neither existent nor non-existent. This is where the thousand sages silently return;
it is where the Buddhas of the three periods eternally abide. It is called the "Heavenly True Buddha-nature" and is also called the "Pure Dharma-body.
To practice apart from this is ultimately to become a follower of demons or external paths.
Question: "The true mind is spiritual awareness; it is so utterly real. The Master said: "The true mind is quiescent illumination, profound and boundless.
The entire world cannot see it; demons and heretics cannot seek it out. Sharp blades cannot wound it; the fires of kalpa cannot burn it.
The Iron Ring Mountains cannot enclose it; the cycle of birth and death cannot drown it. Perfectly round and complete, it has been eternally luminous since antiquity; its brilliance shines forth..."
"Now I am no longer deluded; I have awakened to this true nature of mind. To attain Buddhahood does not depend on the number of kalpas.
The monk asked, "How can one extinguish discursive cognition to achieve spiritual knowledge? How can one transform the deluded mind into the true mind?

The Master said, "Delusion arises from the roots being bound; truth arises from the roots being liberated. [The monk] asked, "How does delusion arise from the roots being bound? How does truth arise from..."

[The Master] explained the faculties and their liberation. The Master said: "Perfectly luminous, empty, and quiescent, there was originally no world, body, or mind. Suddenly and abruptly they arose, and accordingly the faculties and objects were spread out.
Following after objects, one feels aversion and attachment like a moth rushing toward a lamp; pursuing emotions with acceptance and rejection, one is like a silkworm binding itself."

If you can ensure that the faculties do not encounter their objects, the numinous light will naturally shine forth in solitude. If things and self are as one, the six sense-faculties will naturally function interchangeably.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "You need only not follow after movement and stillness, union and separation, tranquility and change, penetration and obstruction."

Darkness arises and light ceases; such are the twelve characteristics of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). By uprooting even one of these, you detach from their stickiness and cause them to subside within.

As they subside and return to the original reality, the fundamental radiance is revealed. Once this luminous nature is made manifest, the remaining five types of stickiness will naturally be completely uprooted and liberated.
This cognitive awareness does not arise from external objects; clarity does not follow the sense organs, yet it manifests by relying upon them.
Thus, the six faculties function as one another’s instruments. Furthermore, Ānanda, if your various faculties were now completely uprooted, their inner luminosity would shine forth.
Such are the ephemeral objects and the vessel-world, along with all their manifested forms; they are like ice melting in hot water, transforming in response to thought.
Regarding this supreme cognitive awareness, you may not yet have awakened to it. I shall once again clearly demonstrate the true mind and the deluded mind, taking cognition as their essence.
The deluded mind relies upon the sense organs and their objects to know through cognition; the true mind is apart from the sense organs and their objects, knowing without cognition.
A beginner who aspires to the Way must clearly discern the distinction between the true and the deluded before applying themselves to practice; then, they will naturally realize sudden enlightenment.
The monk said, "Although I have attained awakening through the instructions you have given above, I am helpless against my heavy karma and restless mind;

my faculties are dull and inferior, and I cannot realize it suddenly. What should I do? The Master said, "By nature, there is fundamentally no awakening; it is because of delusion that there is awakening. By nature, the mind is fundamentally without cultivation;
it is because of defilement that there is cultivation. Therefore, afflictions vary in depth, and habitual tendencies vary in thickness."

Therefore, expedient means are established; there are sudden and gradual methods of cultivation so that those whose defilements are light may suddenly realize perfect penetration, while those whose obstructions are heavy may gradually restore their original nature.
Now, by provisionally employing three faculties, one may enter easily according to one's capacity. Question: What are these three faculties? The Master said:
Those of superior faculty cultivate suddenly; those of middling faculty cultivate gradually; those of inferior faculty cultivate through exertion.
Question: How does one of superior capacity practice through sudden enlightenment? The Master said: One of superior capacity and sharp faculties has cultivated the seeds of the Way in past lives;

upon a single word, their mind-ground opens and penetrates. They maintain this according to conditions, purifying the flowing consciousnesses. When thought moves, they do not allow it to continue; when thought is empty, they do not cling to it.

With a single state of even-mindedness, all things subside of themselves. Whatever meets the eye or encounters the conditions of life is none other than the wondrous function [of the Way]. —Miaoyan of Mount Shishuang.

He said, "If you simply do not let the mind attach to objects, how could objects possibly obstruct a person? He further said, "While every thought-moment clings to conditions, the mind is eternally quiescent;

thus, one realizes the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm and suddenly attains non-arising. If there are those who are dull-witted like roots or trees, he provides expedient means for them to recover gradually.
A monk asked, "Why is it that those who achieve sudden enlightenment and sudden cultivation realize the Way so swiftly? The Master replied, "It is truly so."

This principle is not a false transmission. If this is indeed so, one directly clarifies the mind; through a single thought-moment of perfect cultivation, one attains sudden realization without requiring incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*).
Why wait for the duration of kalpas? The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "For example, suppose there is a person traveling by boat upon the great ocean who wishes to cross it.
If they encounter a favorable wind, they can traverse immeasurable *yojanas* in a mere instant. If...

"Those who do not attain [liberation]" means that although they may dwell for a long time, passing through immeasurable eons, they do not leave their original place. At times, their boat is wrecked and they perish in the water.
Sentient beings are just like this. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Through the illusory samādhi, one transcends the stage of no-more-learning in the snap of a finger.

Therefore, those of the Three Vehicles are ignorant of it, and even those in the Ten Grounds are struck with awe. In a single thought-moment one becomes a Buddha, suddenly transcending kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Question: How does one of medium capacity practice gradually? The Master said: Those of superior capacity practice suddenly, like the wind blowing away clouds so that the bright moon appears in the sky.
Those of medium capacity practice gradually, like polishing a mirror; when the grime is cleared away, the light appears.

If there are later students who have awakened to their original mind, yet whose habitual tendencies from past lives are thick, whose wisdom is inferior, and whose minds are restless, they may, during the twelve periods of the day and night, whether moving or still, [practice as follows...]
Within this, let everything be set down. Do not contemplate good or evil. When a thought arises, be immediately aware of it; once you are aware of it, it vanishes. As the ancient masters said:
"I do not fear the arising of thoughts; I only fear that awakening is late. If you apply yourself with such a mind, after a long time there will be no delusion.

Eventually, when person and dharma both vanish and the faculties and their objects are suddenly cast off, the true mind shines alone, free from obstruction in its expansion or contraction. Question: Regarding the practice of gradual cultivation—

"One may practice seated meditation exclusively, or one may cultivate and realize both movement and stillness. The Master said, "Sudden enlightenment followed by gradual cultivation is more easily accomplished through much stillness.

Those of superior capacity find Chan in both movement and stillness; those of middling capacity abandon worldly affairs to focus exclusively on principle. Indeed, when the practice of sitting becomes thoroughly matured,"
Spontaneously, movement and stillness are without obstruction. A question was asked:
"How should those of inferior capacity exert themselves in cultivation? The Master said: "Those of inferior capacity are dull and ignorant;

their mental faculties are sluggish and hesitant, their torpor is heavy and dense, and their restlessness is fierce and sharp. It is difficult to rouse them through stimulation; they must rely upon guidance, subtle instruction, and assistance from others."
To activate the mechanism [of awakening], those of such caliber must possess faith; do not leave the monastic groves, but always follow a spiritual mentor.

Listen sincerely to their instructions and do not mistake demonic realms for reality. Day after day undergo refinement; moment by moment polish yourself. Repent before the Buddha and humble yourself among the assembly.
After attaining realization, you must not depart from your teacher. Completely renounce the secular world, cultivate deeply, and nurture your practice steadfastly over a long period of time.
Only when one’s conduct corresponds [to the teaching] will there be resonance. A question was asked: "Why is it so laborious to awaken through the lower vehicle's practice?

The Master said: "Because their faculties are dull and their afflictions are thick; because their minds are drowsy and agitated, and their ignorance is heavy. Without bitter refinement, the numinous faculty cannot be awakened. As an ancient worthy said:
'For those of inferior capacity, even with a thousand parables and ten thousand metaphors, they cannot comprehend what is taught. Even if they should attain a slight understanding...'"
Believing themselves to have attained complete enlightenment, they refuse instruction from others and deceive people with their arrogance. Such individuals must give rise to shame;
otherwise, they will become deranged and fall upon a forked path.
Question: For one who has awakened to the principle and maintains it with firm stability, how does one know that the true mind is manifesting before them?

The Master said: "One who has awakened to the principle still has not exhausted their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). When encountering external objects, they may lose mindfulness; therefore, they must nurture [the mind] deeply. It is like herding an ox—one must lead and pull it back."
Whip and subdue it wherever it goes, until the mind is tamed and its steps are steady, so that it no longer harms the crops; only then may you let go of the reins and no longer require a cowherd.
If you wish to test your true mind, go to a place where you are familiar. Seek out things you have always hated or loved and confront them before you. Observe and test them;
if hatred and love arise as before, you will know that the mind has not yet matured. If, however, you encounter...
When one does not give rise to thoughts of hatred or love toward objects that are either adverse or favorable, one knows that the true mind is drawing near and is manifesting.
Even if one intends to give rise again to a heart of attachment by recollecting the pleasures of what was loved, such a heart of attachment and pleasure will not arise at all.
Likewise, even if one intends to give rise again to a heart of aversion by recollecting the anger felt toward what was hated, such a heart of hatred and rage [will not arise].
"Completely unmoving. Only upon reaching this state can one act with mastery according to conditions, responding to things without hindrance. Question:

"Regarding the period before the true mind has manifested and the time when one is resting from delusions while applying effort, it is said that practicing various good deeds simultaneously will cause the path to be easily accomplished.
Is this principle acceptable? The Master said: "Resting the deluded mind is the primary cultivation; performing various good deeds is auxiliary cultivation. If..."
If one performs good deeds with a mind attached to them, one will inevitably fall into the fruits of human and celestial blessings.
If, however, various good deeds are performed without such mental attachment, they may be called auxiliary provisions for right cultivation. As the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:

"Subhūti, when a bodhisattva practices giving without abiding in signs, that merit is inconceivable. Yet, observing those who study today, they are mostly biased and incomplete; few have realized the underlying principle.

Consequently, they rely on their own natural state and do not practice various virtues; thus, their merit is inferior and Māra prevails. Question: "The myriad virtues of conditioned action are blessings and merit (*puṇya*);

seeing one's nature through unconditioned action is spiritual power (*guṇa*). Why, then, do you advocate practicing both, causing them to be intermingled and confused? The Master said: "If conditioned action is attached to, its retribution is that of humans or devas.
If conditioned action is free from defilement, its function manifests the inherent virtue of one's nature."

Question: "Since awakening to the mind and realizing the principle naturally brings about supernatural powers and transformations, why is it that while those who realize the principle today are very numerous, those who possess supernatural powers are extremely few?
The Master said: "Supernatural powers and transformations are merely the branches; one must first establish the root of single-mindedness.
When the root is established, the Way arises, and the powers will manifest spontaneously. If you focus exclusively on supernatural powers and transformations,"
Taking the supreme marks as the Way, even celestial Māras, externalists, malevolent spirits, and divine dragons shall all attain Buddhahood.
If one desires to obtain true supernatural powers, one must realize the Dharma of the One Vehicle. This Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle can give rise to the wondrous function of Prajñā;
it realizes perfect enlightenment within afflictions and attains Nirvāṇa while manifesting in birth and death. Within a single kṣaṇa, it effects transformation.
In all instances of manifesting the holy, there is a transformation within a mere moment that returns to emptiness. Such spiritual transformations cannot be produced by illusory dharmas.

An ancient master said: "There are five kinds of penetration (*abhijñā*): first, the penetration of the Way (*mārga-abhijñā*); second, the penetration of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi-abhijñā*); third, the penetration based on conditions (*āśraya-abhijñā*)."

The fourth is retributive supernatural power (*vipāka-abhijñā*). The fifth is demonic supernatural power (*bhūta-abhijñā*). What is demonic supernatural power? It is when foxes and badgers undergo transformations, or when the spirits of wood and stone manifest;

deities attach themselves to people, making them exceptionally intelligent and strange—this is demonic supernatural power. What is called retributive supernatural power? It is when ghosts and spirits possess foreknowledge.

The transformations of the various devas, the manifestation of birth through the intermediate state (*antarābhava*), and the hidden metamorphoses of divine dragons—these are supernormal powers of retribution (*vipākaja-abhijñā*). What are called supernormal powers based on cultivation (*dharmapratiśaraṇa-abhijñā*)?

They consist of knowing through the application of dharmas, employing them by relying upon the body, traveling back and forth by means of talismans, and the spiritual transformations induced by medicinal herbs; these are supernormal powers based on cultivation.

What is meant by supernormal powers (*abhijñā*)? It is the stilling of the mind to illuminate phenomena, the recollection of past lives, and various forms of discernment—all of which arise from the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

This is called supernormal power. What is meant by the penetration of the Way (*mārga-abhijñā*)? It is responding to phenomena without a [discursive] mind, manifesting through conditions all that exists, like the moon in water or flowers in the sky.
"Reflections have no master; this is the penetration of the Way. When this Way is penetrated, it is true; all other penetrations are false and deceptive.
Being false, they are not true; being deviant, they are not upright. They cause the mind to become deluded and confused, leading one to lose sight of one's original nature.

Therefore, those who truly study the Way do not seek supernatural powers (abhijñā), fearing that they will contravene the True Principle. The *Fuxingji* states: "When one cultivates samādhi, suddenly..."
When supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) arise, one must urgently abandon them, for they are outflows (*āsrava*) and are false and illusory. The *Zhiguan* states that they can obstruct *prajñā*.
Those of inferior capacity falsely seek supernatural powers and take them as the correct path. The Wise One contemplates the true mark of the body; his contemplation of the Buddha is likewise.
It is only when Bodhisattvas of response and transformation, or sages and worthies who have realized the principle, manifest miraculous transformations at the very end [of their careers] that—
They do not dwell in the world. If they were to appear in the world to manifest their transformations and convert the masses, these would be nothing other than *yakṣas* or demonic enchantments.

Question: For those who have not yet attained awakening, they are deluded regarding the truth and pursue the false; they create causes of good and evil and receive the fruits of suffering and joy, taking birth according to their karma—of this principle there is no doubt.
However, for those who have awakened to the principle, they suddenly restore their true mind, transcend all causes and effects, and sever all [bonds].
[Question: "When this single spirit departs from the body, upon what can it rely? The Master said: "All sentient beings receive fruits according to their causes;

that which arises through conditions may be called a reliance. However, those who have awakened to the mind and realized the Way are not like the worldly wanderers drifting and adrift, or like the masterless, solitary ghosts of the realm of spirits, wandering aimlessly without any support."
As for the locus: if one awakens to the fundamental principle such that it manifests before one, then the four quarters, above and below, are all the true mind.
This is the total utilization of the entire body; there is no other place upon which to rely. An ancient worthy said, "The entire earth is the single eye of a śramaṇa.
He also said, "The entire earth is a monastery. Minister Wen Cao asked Guifeng, "Regarding the awakening to principle..."

When such a person’s single lifetime comes to an end, upon what can they rely? Guifeng said: "All sentient beings are without exception endowed with the numinous, luminous, and awakened nature, which is no different from that of the Buddha.
If one can awaken to this nature, it is the Dharmakāya; being fundamentally unborn from the beginning, how could there be anything upon which to rely?
This numinous luminosity is never obscured; it is a constant, clear awareness that comes from nowhere and likewise goes nowhere."
That which departs has emptiness and stillness as its very essence. Do not identify with the physical body; take spiritual awareness as your own mind. Do not identify with deluded thoughts.
If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. Then, at the time of death, karma will naturally be unable to bind you.
Even if there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), your destination will be autonomous. Whether in the heavens or among humans, you may dwell wherever you wish. All things—

When the subtle, continuous flow is exhausted into emptiness, there remains only the luminous illumination of the great wisdom of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*). According to the capacities of beings, it transforms and delivers those with karmic affinity, leading them to awaken to the mind and realize the principle, so that they may together attain the Buddha-way.

Question: In antiquity, there were eminent monks who remained seated in a state of transformation (sitting-meditation until death), their bodies remaining intact for many years without decay, while their hair and nails grew naturally.
I do not yet understand what principle underlies this path. The Master said: This is the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) practice of abiding in the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

It merely ceases the six consciousnesses; the eighth consciousness maintains the body. All such practitioners do so because they loathe the realm of existence and seek emptiness, temporarily seeking rest. Although they enter this absorption, their life-span—
The heat does not perish; later, consciousness arises, like a tertian fever. One must awaken to the certainty of the nature [of reality] before one can escape saṃsāra. Question:

Does the extinction-attainment (nirodha-samāpatti) attained by Mahākāśyapa and the extinction-attainment of the Hīnayāna differ, or are they the same? Master: In the Mahāyāna, it is the extinction of principle (li);

in the Hīnayāna, it is the extinction of phenomena (shi). The extinction in the Mahāyāna is complete because, while possessing the five aggregates, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses are able to induce it.

Regarding dignified deportment (*īryāpatha*): in the [Mahayana], it is unimpeded whether in meditative concentration or in distraction, and principle and phenomena are not discarded. Although the Hinayana possesses physical conduct, because the first six consciousnesses have already been suppressed and extinguished, its deportment is incomplete;
concentration and distraction are not perfected, and while phenomena are discarded, it is one-sidedly quiescent. Therefore, their concentrations are not the same.

The monk asked, "As extensively shown above, regarding the distinctions among the vehicles of teaching, those of late learning who encounter the gateway of sudden enlightenment will surely understand it clearly. Yet, are there still distinctions within the teachings and principles?
I beg you again for a subtle and detailed exposition. The Master said, "If there is a question, there shall be an answer; thus I shall not fail the potential of one who has come to me."
Question: Why is it called "the myriad dharmas returning to the mind"? The Master said: It is like gold following a craftsman to become many kinds of vessels;
when all the vessels enter the furnace, they melt away and become one body. The myriad dharmas returning to the mind is also like this.
Question: What superior power does the Dharma-gate of sudden enlightenment possess? The Master said: "With correct understanding and perfect cultivation, its power transcends the span of kalpas.
Though remaining within birth and death, one constantly enters nirvana; though perpetually dwelling amidst worldly toil, one eternally resides in the Pure Land.

Possessing the physical eye, one opens the wisdom-eye; transforming the ordinary mind, one becomes identical with the Buddha-mind. One should know that the merit and virtue of sudden enlightenment are supreme and vast. Question: [Regarding] clarifying the mind...
"Seeing one's nature is like a person drinking water; whether it is cold or warm, they know it for themselves. This statement also lacks any external basis. The Master said:
"When a student applies their mind with intimacy and investigates the reality, suddenly body and mind become as one, and the light of wisdom is instantly manifested.

One pierces through to the state prior to the empty kalpa and personally arrives at the ground of original enlightenment. It is difficult to speak of with words and difficult to describe with a brush. It is like a person..."

When drinking water, one knows its coldness or warmth for oneself. Yet, if one wishes to employ skillful means to reveal the original mind, one must rely upon the vehicles of the teachings (*śāsana-yāna*) and utilize metaphors through indirect access.

Question: The opening instructions of the Zen school do not permit the study of the teachings; yet, if one were to gain even a partial understanding from them, would this not result in becoming self-satisfied with mere literary knowledge?

The student asked, "Is this consciousness true or false? The Master said, "If you wish to study the teachings (*śāstra-yāna*) and explore the precious treasury, you must resolve every point back to your own self and ensure every word accords with your original mind.
However, I fear that by clinging to the literal text, you will give rise to intellectual interpretations and refuse to realize the fundamental essence.
This is why I mock those who study the teachings and thereby become mere 'sages of words. The student asked, "What is delusion? What is awakening? The Master said:
It arises from the fundamental true mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-bodhi*). Non-enlightenment is called delusion; through non-enlightenment, initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) is achieved.
Returning to the true mind is called awakening. Therefore it is said: "One falls because of the ground, and one rises again because of the ground.

Although delusion and awakening differ, the true mind is non-dual. Question: Why must both the real and the false be extinguished by one who accords with the principle? The Master said: Because... [text ends]

To falsely speak of "truth" is to say that truth has no self-characteristic; from truth arises delusion, yet the essence of delusion is fundamentally empty. Since delusion is fundamentally empty, truth likewise cannot be established.
When both truth and delusion are simultaneously extinguished, the fundamental mind abides eternally.
Question: In the Gate of the Patriarchs, there is sudden enlightenment and a direct entry with a single blade; why then is it necessary to use language to extensively discuss distinctions?

The Master said: A practitioner who investigates the mystery must possess two eyes. The first is the eye of self, which clarifies the fundamental principle; the second is the eye of wisdom, which discerns delusion. As the Chan school says:
"To clarify only oneself while failing to comprehend what is before one's eyes—such a person possesses only a single eye, and their realization is isolated."

If one focuses solely on phenomena, one will ultimately fail to achieve universal penetration. If considering wisdom to be wrong, then the Greatly Wise Mañjuśrī would not be called the Son of the Dharma King.
If considering the cessation of study to be right, then the monk Wuwen would not have become a person in hell.
All are due to the lock of the mental consciousness; it is difficult to open without the key of wisdom. One may say that emotional thoughts entangle one another;
they cannot be severed without the sword of insight. Those who advance in the cultivation of perfect penetration must not harbor views that transcend words.

Question: Does the practice and realization of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun) still fall within the realm of cause and effect? The Master said: "From the Buddhas above down to sentient beings below, all are encompassed by cause and effect;
how could one possibly deny this? It is only because non-Buddhists do not understand dependent origination and cling exclusively to the doctrine of spontaneity (svabhāva)."

They deny cause and effect. Those of the Two Vehicles are like those with impaired vision; they merely realize partial emptiness and, through the extinction of wisdom and the dissolution of the body, distance themselves from cause and effect.
Ordinary beings are bound by karma and crave the five desires; as their bodies are burned in the house on fire, they cling to cause and effect—both result in nothing but deluded understandings.
Having personally been obscured from the perfect and eternal, you take only the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) as the cause and the true mark as the fruit.
Do not harbor views that negate existence and thereby fall into heterodox paths; rather, suddenly establish the perfect cause and suddenly realize the wondrous fruit.
Question: In the world there are gentlemen who accord with the Principle, whom they call "path-makers without mind. If they are without mind, they would be like wood or stone.
Why then do the sages and worthies possess great wisdom? The Master said: A path-maker without mind is not the same as wood or stone.
They have no discriminating mind, no mind of aversion or attachment, no mind of grasping or rejecting, no mind of good or evil, and no mind of emptiness or existence. They have no—

A mind that is neither middle nor extreme; a mind without interior or exterior; a mind without attachment. Yet this is not a mind devoid of spiritual awareness, but rather the true mind of tranquil illumination.
Question: An ancient said, "Do not say that being 'without mind' is itself the Way; even 'no-mind' still leaves one separated by a further barrier.

What does this mean? The Master said: "The true mind is void and profound; it is neither existent nor non-existent. To discard existence and dwell in non-existence is, on the contrary, a great error. [He recited] an ancient master’s verse:
It is said: I exhort you to study the Way and not harbor greedy desires; when all things are free from the mind, one reaches the ultimate point.
Only by being without mind does one realize the Way of no-mind; once this no-mind is realized, even that "no" ceases.
Question: What is meant by "knowing through non-knowing" and "non-knowing while knowing"? The Master said: Non-knowing is the essence of the mind; knowing is the function of the mind.
The essence can give rise to function—this is "knowing through non-knowing. Function does not depart from the essence—this is "non-knowing while knowing.
If function were to depart from the essence, it would be a state of abiding in characteristics. If the essence were without function, it would be called "stolid emptiness."

Question: What is meant by having mindfulness and yet knowing it as delusion? The Master said: When the six sense organs encounter their objects, thoughts are stirred and discrimination arises; because one knows with mindfulness, it is considered delusion. Question: What is meant by knowing without a mind and being thus true? The Master said: The true mind responds to things like a mirror reflecting images; because one knows without a mind, it is considered true. Question: What is correct knowing? The Master said: It is like the empty sky responding to the myriad forms; it is neither existent nor non-existent. This is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when the four elements are exhausted and the five aggregates perish, the body returns to the earth and the spirit returns to the void. At that time, there is no longer any distinction between self and other, nor any further arising of thoughts. This is called correct knowing. Moreover, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the three realms of existence, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense objects, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense organs, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six consciousnesses, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense fields, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense bases, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense faculties, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense powers, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense functions, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense activities, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense perceptions, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense cognitions, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense knowledges, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense understandings, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense realizations, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense attainments, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense accomplishments, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense fulfillments, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense completions, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense consummations, this is called correct knowing. Furthermore, when one does not give rise to thoughts regarding the six sense perfections, this is called correct knowing.
