The Ten Demons Disturb the Right Teacher, who said: "Awakening and practicing *dhyāna* is no trivial matter. When internal and external demons disturb right concentration, one lacks mastery;
becoming attached to objects of desire and being shaken by those objects, one falls into the net of demons. What was originally a wholesome cause instead leads to calamity."

Evil fruits [result from this]. Those who are beginners and those of later generations must be cautious and guard themselves against them. I, a fool, shall set forth ten points to distinguish the meaning of demons (*māra*). Examine and scrutinize yourself;

regarding both mental demons and celestial demons, employ the observation of wisdom (*prajñā*) to eliminate demonic calamities. If the defilements of the mind are purified, all obstacles will naturally vanish.
Why fear celestial demons? How could they dare to delude the upright? I shall now describe these ten demons in detail below. First:
First, karmic resentment from past lives; second, external distractions; third, afflictions (*kleśa*); fourth, cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*); fifth, false views; sixth, deluded thoughts;
seventh, verbal karma; eighth, the suffering of illness; ninth, mental dullness and torpor; tenth, the celestial Māras. These ten demonic obstacles can disturb correct cultivation.
Those who aspire to the Way should regard them with gravity and exercise the utmost caution.
Question: What is meant by "karmic demons from past enmity"? The Master said: "Karmic demons from past enmity" refers to karmic obstructions (*karmāvaraṇa*).

From distant kalpas until this present life, while in the state of an ordinary being, one was unfilial and undutiful, lacking benevolence and righteousness; one committed killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying, and through greed, anger, ignorance, and attachment, one formed many enemies.
When encountering these in the present life, they disturb and unsettle one who wishes to study the Great Way, and are able to obstruct the realization of the Holy Path.

If one's affairs do not reach fulfillment, one must give rise to shame and remorse, earnestly praying and repenting, and seeking the compassionate protection of the Triple Gem through their divine power.
Then all past karma will naturally dissipate and vanish, and all enemies will naturally retreat and disperse.

One should again make four vows to universally benefit all sentient beings, swiftly attaining the state of non-outflow and quickly realizing Bodhi. Those who practice Chan meditation must personally repent.

Question: What is meant by "external delusive demons"? The Master said: External delusive demons refer to human obstacles—namely, icchantikas and petty people, regardless of whether they are noble or lowly—who disturb the concentrated mind and prevent it from attaining stability.
Because there is no distinction between them, they are all [manifestations of] the Lesser [Vehicle].

As for the reasons they are not summoned: perhaps they lack ritual propriety and righteousness; perhaps they are self-exalting; perhaps they are arrogant; perhaps their speech is blunt; perhaps their conduct is coarse; perhaps they rely on their power;
perhaps they boast of their talent; perhaps their words are malicious; perhaps they praise their own abilities; perhaps they discuss the faults of others;
perhaps they have little harmony in their countenance; perhaps they lack reverence; perhaps their measure is not broad; or perhaps they lack patience. For these reasons, they are not summoned.
Faith. Delusive confusion obstructs practice; the stirring of thoughts and the movement of the mind veil the fundamental luminosity.

Those who aspire to the Way must humble themselves, withdrawing from self-importance to nurture virtue, thereby avoiding the obstacles posed by others. For those newly entering the study, one must be broad-minded and patient.
Question: What is meant by the "demon of afflictions" (kleśamāra)? The Master said: The demon of afflictions refers to obstacles to practice.
If these obstacles to practice are not removed, they can disturb correct cultivation. What is meant by "affliction" (fan)? What is meant by "disturbance" (nǎo)?

Affliction pursues external objects; disturbance arises within the internal mind. Those who cultivate dhyāna must certainly sever them. If they are not suddenly eliminated, the fundamental nature will be difficult to manifest. Upon seeing a woman...

The mind: the affliction of lustful thoughts upon seeing [objects of] desire; the affliction of malicious thoughts upon seeing the killing of living beings; the affliction of covetous thoughts upon seeing wealth;

the affliction of thieving thoughts upon seeing property; the affliction of greed upon seeing people; the affliction of the mark of selfhood (*ātman*) arising as pride upon seeing those superior to oneself;

the affliction of arrogance arising as haughtiness upon seeing those inferior to oneself; the affliction of resentment arising as anger upon seeing those who oppose one; and the affliction of following one's whims arising as joy upon seeing those who comply.

Affliction (*kleśa*). Seeing an enemy gives rise to hatred; this is the affliction of resentment. Seeing a relative gives rise to attachment; this is the affliction of partiality. All external perceptions give rise internally to grasping and rejecting;
these are all afflictions. They are difficult to describe exhaustively. Those who practice Chan meditation must certainly eliminate the obstacles of phenomena (*vastu-āvaraṇa*).
If the obstacles of phenomena are not emptied, they will disturb right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*). How can those of later generations not sever them?
Question: What is meant by the "demon of the knowable"? The Master said: The demon of the knowable refers to the obstruction of principle (*dharmāvaraṇa*).

If this obstruction of principle is not eliminated, it can disturb right concentration. What is this "knowable" that constitutes such a fault? It is knowing that one has attained enlightenment; knowing that one has penetrated the essential school;

knowing that one understands the teachings; knowing that one has realized the principle; knowing that one possesses extensive learning; knowing that one has many insights; and knowing that one maintains the precepts.

Yan, you know that I have attained samādhi; you know that I possess wisdom; you know that I have realized emptiness; you know that I am sovereign; you know that I am unimpeded; you know that I have attained supernatural powers;
you know that I have attained the sublime; you know that I have realized the Way; you know that I have become a Buddha—and such things as these that you know become obstacles to the Principle.
If these obstacles to the Principle are not removed, attachment to phenomena (dharmagrāha) will not be forgotten. If attachment to phenomena is not forgotten, the True Mind will not [manifest].
Manifestation. Those who practice meditative concentration must necessarily obliterate it.
Question: What is meant by the demon of false views? The Master said: The demon of false views refers to the obstruction of attachment.

If this obstruction is not removed, one will inevitably fall into a state of perverted concentration. What constitutes false views? To thus disrupt the correct [path] while clinging to one's nature without letting go—this is called "existence."

To perceive [existence] and cling to its nature as fundamentally empty is called the view of non-existence (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). To cling to it as fundamentally immortal is called the view of permanence (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).

To cling to it as perishing along with the vital breath is called the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). To cling to the arising of what was previously non-existent is the view of spontaneity (*svabhāva-dṛṣṭi*). To cling to the transformation of the vital breath into form is the view of false causes (*mithyā-hetu-dṛṣṭi*).

When one realizes that suchness is neither existent nor non-existent, yet is both existent and non-existent, all false attachments and false views, along with their causal conditions, naturally [cease].

However, if one does not depart from emptiness and existence, or from the two extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, one will obstruct the fundamental principle for oneself and fall onto a forked path.
Those who practice Chan meditation must understand this through awakening.
Question: What is meant by the "demon of deluded thought" (*vikalpa-māra*)? The Master said: The demon of deluded thought refers to self-obstruction.

When self-obstruction is not empty, arising and ceasing ceaselessly, and inverted thoughts and distractions scatter about, they obstruct the fundamental mind. Those who practice Zen must necessarily empty this.

Now, I shall cite one or two instances to clarify these delusive obstructions: deluded thought regarding the realization of the Way, deluded thought regarding cultivation and realization, and deluded thought regarding attainment.

Meditative concentration; deluded thoughts giving rise to wisdom; deluded thoughts possessing extensive knowledge; deluded thoughts being skilled in literature; deluded thoughts being called "attained";
deluded thoughts receiving many offerings; deluded thoughts acting as teachers; deluded thoughts being venerated by the multitude; deluded thoughts continuing the ancestral lineage;

deluded thoughts dwelling in Buddha-lands; deluded thoughts propagating the Way; deluded thoughts transmitting records; deluded thoughts being the progeny; deluded thoughts entering the Tripitaka; deluded thoughts possessing supernatural powers; deluded thoughts regarding the profound mystery.

Exquisite! These are extraordinary delusions; they are strange and bizarre delusions. They are delusions of immortality, delusions of returning to childhood, delusions of ascending to heaven, and delusions of attaining Buddhahood.
All such delusions are not empty; yet every stirring of thought deviates from the Truth. For those who have newly begun to study the Way, the eradication of delusion must be the foundation.
Question: What is meant by the demon of verbal karma (*vākkarman-māra*)? The Master said: The demon of verbal karma refers to the obstacle of madness.

If one does not exercise restraint over speech but indulges in excessive talk, with a distracted mind and chaotic thoughts, one cannot attain a concentrated mind. For what reason does verbal karma exceed all others in its severity?

It is because people discuss the profound and the subtle, lecture on the teachings and their essential principles, boast of their own realization, disparage others as ignorant and deluded, and debate the virtues of others.

Briefly stated: they speak of others' right and wrong; they compose poems, songs, and rhapsodies; they sing out recklessly and at random; they pass judgment on the past and present; they debate the rise and fall of nations;
they discuss the wise and foolish of former days and the malevolent and virtuous of today; they engage in lofty discourse and contentious arguments regarding matters that do not concern themselves;

they gratuitously disparage or praise the gains and losses of others; they describe various objects of desire, inciting people to love; and they speak of various injustices, provoking people to anger.

Anger; slandering behind one’s back or criticizing to one’s face; and all manner of words regarding profit or loss that cause others to lose right mindfulness—these must be strictly avoided by those who practice Chan meditation.
Not only should one be sparing with speech to nourish virtue, but one must also ensure the mind remains undisturbed.
Beginners on the path of cultivation should be cautious of and guard against these things.
Question: What is meant by the demon of the suffering of illness? The Master replied: The demon of the suffering of illness refers to the obstacle of suffering.

When the body is plagued by many diseases, it is all due to karmic transgressions; or perhaps one’s own internal harmony has been lost, causing a hundred ailments to arise, such that one cannot enjoy [the fruits of practice] and there are hindrances to studying the Way.

I, your humble servant, shall set forth several points for you to prevent [illness] yourself: regulate the spleen and stomach, be discerning regarding food and drink, and do not greedily crave rich flavors.
Regarding flavors: avoid cold and raw foods. Do not recite scriptures when hungry; do not carry heavy loads when full. Do not sleep immediately after eating. At night, avoid eating to satiety.
One has a fondness for rotten food, a craving for fried and stir-fried dishes, and a particular greed for the five tastes.

One forcibly uses improper items, sits in meditation on damp ground, dozes off in windy places, enters water while perspiring, craves coolness during the heat, bathes against the wind, and sleeps out in the open under the stars.
Below. Excessive hunger and excessive satiety; excessive joy and excessive anger; extreme cold and extreme heat; heavy rain and heavy dew;

internal injuries and external pathogens—when all these lose their harmony, various sores and illnesses arise, causing the body to be ill at ease. Those who study later must know this and take precautions to avoid it.
Question: What is meant by the demon of lethargy (*styāna-māra*)? The Master said: The demon of lethargy refers to the obstacle of sleep.

If this obstacle of sleep is not refined away, lethargy becomes too heavy; the true mind does not shine forth, and the nature of wisdom does not manifest. One falls into obscurity, into the dark mountain caves of demons. What is the cause of this illness?
It is largely due to this obstacle of lethargy, which stems from heavy eating and an excessive craving for rich flavors. Excessive talk leads to ruin.

When the vital energy (*qi*) is exhausted, the spleen becomes weary and the spirit lacks clarity; turbid energies become chaotic, leading to much delusion and anger, as well as indolence and negligence.
One fails to contemplate birth and death, craving only ease and comfort. Those who study later in life must exert themselves with diligence:

they should prick their flesh with needles, strike their heads against pillars, prostrate before the Buddha, light lamps, stand upon precipices, practice walking meditation, and subject their bodies to ascetic refinement until sleep itself becomes a source of distress.
If one is negligent and allows the mind to run wild, the true mind will not be luminous. Those who practice Chan must courageously subdue it.
Question: What is meant by the "great celestial Māra"? The Master said: The great celestial Māra is not like other obstacles;

rather, he arises because, while practicing correctly with the intent to realize the Way, the mind becomes so refined and harmonious that it remains profoundly still and unmoving. This startles the celestial Māras and various ghosts into manifesting.
The divine palaces split asunder and the great earth shook; the Demon King was struck with terror and the malevolent spirits fled in panic.
All the demonic enchanters, possessing the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*), came together to cause disturbance, seeking to prevent entry into the state of sagehood.

They manifested various strange anomalies and transformed themselves into objects of desire to disrupt your meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*). As the mind gave rise to grasping and rejecting, the demons seized the opportunity; the master suffered harm and fell into madness.
To be mad is to have already attained Buddhahood for oneself; yet one may fall into royal peril while alive and descend into the Avīci Hell after death.

For those who practice Zen, right mindfulness is distinct and wisdom shines brightly; with the single mind unmoving, they remain indifferent to whatever others may do to them, seeing and hearing nothing. Through right concentration, demons are subdued and naturally extinguished.
Those of later generations who cultivate the Way should be careful to discern this for themselves.

The above points briefly enumerate the activities of Māra. To discern them thoroughly and in detail, one must study the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding internal and external demonic afflictions and all heterodox views, understanding each one clearly.
Only then, when applying effort in practice, will one not fall into the net of Māra and directly realize the fruit of Buddhahood.
The scriptural citations state:
"The myriad dharmas return to the mind. This question and answer is clear and distinct; those of superior capacity, upon merely glancing at it, suddenly awaken to their original mind.

Those of middling or inferior capacity, being deluded and dull-witted, harbor doubts, slander it, and do not believe. Therefore, the words of the Buddhas and patriarchs from the sutras are cited as proof to sever all doubts and inspire sincere faith.

This is erroneous. Yet there are those who attain awakening and, relying on the teachings, practice accordingly; they enter directly into the groves of the ancient Buddhas and transcend horizontally across the threshold of the patriarchs.
This may be called attaining the Buddha-eye through the fleshly eye and manifesting the true mind through the ordinary mind.
Now, I shall recount the words of the Buddha and the patriarchs to provide印证 (yìnzhèng) and confirm the correct principle of returning to the mind.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "All Tathāgatas abide together in one place; they are intrinsically pure and subsumed within the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*).
The *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states: "Regarding the Dharma taught through words and phrases, those of small intelligence engage in false discrimination.
Consequently, obstacles arise; they do not understand their own minds. Failing to understand their own minds, how could they know the right path? That...
Through perverted perceptions, one increases all evils. The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states: "The ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is that there is only mind;

all various external appearances are entirely non-existent. Those foolish people, clinging to evil views, deceive themselves and others, and are unable to clearly see the true abiding place of all phenomena as they really are. Mahāmati, regarding all phenomena..."
"Reality as it is" means being able to thoroughly comprehend that all which appears is manifested solely by the mind.
The *Sutra in Forty-two Sections* says: "Those who have left the household life as śramaṇas sever desire and abandon attachment;

they recognize the source of their own minds, realize the fundamental principle of the Buddhas, and awaken to the dharma of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). Within, there is nothing to be attained; without, there is nothing to be sought. The mind is not bound to the Path, nor..."

It is not an action that binds; it is without thought and without fabrication. It is neither cultivated nor realized, and it does not pass through the various stages, yet it is naturally most exalted;
this is called the Way (*mārga*). The *Ratnamegha Sūtra* states: "Of all dharmas, the mind is the foremost. If one knows the mind, then one can know [all things]."

Regarding all phenomena, a verse from the *Kāraṇaprajñapti-sūtra* states: "All acts of creating good and evil arise from the mind and its perceptions; therefore, for those who have truly left the household life, the clarification of the mind is fundamental."
The *Bodhisattva-nien-fo-san-mei-jing* (Sutra on the Bodhisattva’s Samādhi of Mindfulness of the Buddha) states: "The mind is like a vajra, for its roots of goodness penetrate all phenomena.
The mind is like a kālinjara cloth, for its roots of goodness are supple and soft. The mind is like the great ocean, for its roots of goodness encompass the entire collection of precepts.
The mind is like a level stone, for its roots of goodness sustain all undertakings. The mind is like the king of mountains... [and so forth].
Because the faculties give rise to all wholesome dharmas, the mind is like the great earth. Because the roots of goodness sustain the activities of sentient beings, the *Samādhi-sūtra* says:
"That which, in meditative concentration, is unattached to the internal or external, nor to that which lies between them—this is called single-mindedness (*ekāgratā*)."

The *Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra* states: Mañjuśrī addressed the Venerable Śāriputra, "Just as the fires of the kalpa of destruction, blazing for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges, can never burn empty space;

even so, Śāriputra, though each and every sentient being may commit the crimes of immediate retribution and unwholesome karma for eons as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, their fundamental nature of mind can never be defiled."
The verses from the *Ākāśagarbha-paripṛcchā-sūtra* state: "Space is free from arising and ceasing; the dharma-realm has no coming or going.
All forms appear within space, and all phenomena abide dependent upon the mind. Space is neither form nor non-form; the nature of the mind is likewise so.
'Space' is merely a conventional designation; the same applies to the mind, intellect, and consciousness."
A verse from the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra says: "All phenomena have no intrinsic nature; they are said to be mind-only. Failing to perceive one's own mind, one gives rise to conceptual discrimination."
The *Chuyao jing* (Udānavarga) states: "One whose body is clad in the armor of the precepts but whose mind lacks the sword of wisdom cannot destroy the head of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
Thus we know that if one does not contemplate the mind, and thus fails to achieve sublime wisdom, one cannot sever the root of ignorance."
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that "lion’s roar" refers to definitively proclaiming that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
If one knows that the Buddha-nature is fully present within one's own mind, then how could there be any dharma outside of this nature that could be sought?
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi Sūtra* states: "Without attachment and without dependence, free from entanglements and with a tranquil mind, one's original nature is like empty space;
this is called the Unsurpassed Way."
The Verses of the Seven Buddhas.
The verse of Vipaśyin Buddha says: "The body receives birth from within the signless, Just like various forms produced by illusion.
The mind-consciousness of the illusory person is originally non-existent; Both sin and merit are empty, with nothing in which to abide."
The verse of Śikhin Buddha says: "The arising of all wholesome dharmas is fundamentally an illusion; the commissioning of all unwholesome karmas is likewise an illusion.
The body is like a mass of foam, the mind is like the wind; they are illusory manifestations, rootless and devoid of real nature."
The verse by Vipaśyin Buddha says: "Borrowing the four great elements to form a body, The mind is originally unborn, arising only due to objects.
If the external object is absent, the mind is likewise non-existent; Transgressions and blessings are like illusions—arising and then ceasing."
The verse of Krakucchanda Buddha says: "To see that the body has no reality is the Buddha’s vision; to realize that the mind is like an illusion is the Buddha’s realization.
Having realized that the fundamental nature of both body and mind is empty—how can such a person differ from the Buddha?"
The verse by the Buddha Kanakamuni states: "The Buddha does not perceive a body to know he is the Buddha; if there were truly a knowing apart from this, there would be no Buddha.
The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; thus they remain composed and unafraid of birth and death."
The verse of Kāśyapa Buddha says: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning, they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit."
The verse by Śākyamuni Buddha says: "Illusions have no cause and are without birth; they are all seen as such through spontaneity.
All phenomena are nothing other than self-transformed births; illusions being unborn, there is nothing to fear."
The Buddhist scriptures have already clarified this;
the Patriarchal words describe it further. The verse of the First Patriarch says: "Neither do I behold evil and give rise to aversion; Nor do I observe good and strive to cultivate it.
I neither abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, Nor do I cast off delusion to pursue enlightenment. To realize the Great Way is to transcend measure and penetrate the Buddha."
The mind issues forth deliverance; it does not share the same entanglements as ordinary beings or sages. Transcending all, it is called the Patriarch. The Second Patriarch said:
"This mind is the Buddha; this mind is the Dharma. Dharma and Buddha are non-dual; so too is the Jewel of the Sangha."
The Third Patriarch said: "If the eye does not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord. If the mind does not differ, the myriad dharmas are as one.
When this oneness embodies the profound mystery, one becomes motionless and forgets external conditions. When the myriad dharmas are viewed as equal, one returns to and rests in spontaneity."
The Fourth Patriarch said to Great Master Rong: "A hundred thousand wondrous gates all return to the single square inch of the mind;
the merits of the Ganges sands are all contained within the original source of the heart. All gates of concentration, all gates of wisdom, and all gates of practice are fully present therein.
Supernatural powers and wondrous functions are likewise entirely within your own mind."
The Fifth Patriarch said: "If you wish to know the essential teaching of the Dharma, the mind is the root of the twelve divisions of the scriptures.
There is only the One Vehicle Dharma; that which is the One Vehicle Dharma is simply the one mind. Merely maintaining the one mind is the gate of the true suchness of the mind.
All dharmas and practices do not transcend one's own mind; they are known only by the mind itself. The mind has no form or color; the patriarchs have transmitted it solely through the mind."
The mind. Those who have attained realization confirm this;
there is no other dharma. The Sixth Patriarch said: "All of you, your own minds are the Buddha. Do not harbor further doubt. Outside the mind, there is not a single dharma that can be established;
all are the myriad kinds of dharmas produced from the mind. As the sutra says: "The mind gives rise to all manner of dharmas."
Birth: its nature is non-dual, and the mind is likewise so. Its Way is pure and free from all marks. Do not contemplate purity, nor empty the mind;
this mind is non-dual and beyond acceptance or rejection. Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, if the mind is always straightforward, that itself is the Pure Land.
Those who rely upon my words will surely attain Bodhi.

The *Jueguan lun* (Treatise on the Cessation of Contemplation) by Great Master Niutou Rong. Question: What is this mind? Answer: That which is observed by the six sense faculties is entirely the mind.

Master Chou said: "All external conditions are called 'having no fixed characteristics. Right and wrong, arising and ceasing, all stem from one's own mind.
If the mind itself is not a mind, who would find fault with right and wrong? When both subject and object are absent, all phenomena are eternally quiescent."

Master Pang’s verse says: "The myriad dharmas arise from the mind; the mind arising, the myriad dharmas arise. If one does not realize the non-existence of this constant arising, one travels in vain through coming and going.

Fudō emerges from the deep pit. Master Tengteng sang:
"To cultivate the Way, there is no Way to cultivate; to inquire about the Dharma, there is no Dharma to inquire about. Deluded people do not awaken to the emptiness of form;
the enlightened have fundamentally neither opposition nor compliance. Of the eighty-four thousand gates of Dharma, the ultimate principle does not exceed this."
Within the square inch of the heart, afflictions are precisely bodhi. Pure flowers grow from mud and dung. Recognize the city of your own home;
do not wander idly through other provinces.
Master Wolun said: "Examine the nature of the mind: it is as profound and still as empty space; fundamentally unborn, it likewise does not perish. Why must you suppress it?
Whenever you perceive the mind arise, you must immediately turn the light inward to reflect upon the source of the mind.
It has no root; thus, there is no place of birth. Because there is no place of birth, the mind is tranquil, signless, and unconditioned."
Chan Master Zhida’s *Verses on the Mind and Objects* state: When objects arise, the mind exists; when the mind is absent, objects do not arise.

If one binds the mind to objects, both mind and object become blind. When objects and mind each abide in themselves, the nature of mind and object is eternally pure. Awakening to objects, the mind does not arise; delusion regarding objects, the mind acts in tandem with them.
If one is deluded and takes the mind to be the object, then mind and object will be in disarray,纵横 (zōnghéng—crosswise and lengthwise). Awakening to objects...

The source of the mind is pure; know that the nature of the mind's objects is fundamentally clear. Know that the mind has no objective realm as its essence, and realize that the objective realm has no form within the mind.
The realm is empty and the mind is tranquil; the mind illuminates the realm and the realm is cool and still.
The Great Master Puan said: "The Great Way is vast and empty; there is only the single true mind. Do not contemplate good or evil;
the spirit is pure beyond all things—what more is there to worry about?"
Master Guishan said: "Know that all internal and external phenomena are entirely unreal; they are born through the transformation of the mind and are all merely provisional names.
Let the nature of phenomena flow freely as it may; neither sever it nor continue it."
Master Huangbo said: "Simply awaken to the one mind; there is not the slightest dharma that can be attained. This is the true Buddha.
Between the Buddha and sentient beings, the one mind is no different. Rather than [seeking elsewhere], recognize your own fundamental Dharma at this very moment.
This Dharma is the mind; outside the mind there is no Dharma. This mind is the Dharma; outside the Dharma there is no mind."

Master Yangshan said: "To suddenly awaken to one's own mind as being without marks, like empty space, and for that which is manifested through the sense organs to be the fundamental mind itself, possessing wondrous functions as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—having nothing else to support it and nothing else to establish it—is the original ground; it is the original land."
Master Anguo said: The Sutra says, "One should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere.
To dwell nowhere means not to dwell on form, not to dwell on sound, not to dwell on delusion, not to dwell on enlightenment, not to dwell on essence, and not to dwell on function.
"To give rise to the mind" means that the One Mind is manifested in all places. If one dwells on goodness and gives rise to the mind, it manifests as goodness. If...

When one dwells in evil, the mind of evil arises and manifests; the original mind then becomes obscured. If there is no dwelling, then throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is only this single mind.
One can then believe and know that it is not the wind or the banner that moves, but rather this mind that moves.
Master Guizong said: "The very mind is Buddha. Thoroughly penetrating, there is only nature (*dharmatā*). Mountains, rivers, and the great earth are all sealed by this single Dharma;
it is a great divine mantra, true and not false. It is the fundamental source of all Buddhas and the very marrow of Bodhi.
What is this Buddha? It is right here, at this very moment—there is no other person. As a sutra says: 'For example, like a single form...'"
Sentient beings perceive it and obtain various names; yet all phenomena are but a single phenomenon, receiving different names according to their respective locations.
As a verse in the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states: "Just as space pervades everything, yet space is without discrimination, so too is the stainless mind of one's own nature."
It is likewise universally non-conceptual.
Again, he paid homage to the Dharma Master and said: "Regarding the meaning of karma: karma arises from the mind; the mind is the function of karma.
Karma leads the mind to receive a physical form, and the mind follows karma to create its objects. Thus, one receives a body because of karma, and that body in turn creates karma."
The mind creates objects, and objects in turn give rise to the mind; it is like shadows following forms in their curvature or straightness, and echoes following sounds in their volume or smallness.

Now, to expound the True Dharma brings merit exceeding that of the sands of the Ganges; to transmit the ultimate principle brings benefit surpassing that of the great void.
The sands of the Ganges are countless, and the great void is boundless; yet the merit of bestowing the Dharma to benefit sentient beings exceeds these two metaphors.
Why is this merit so immeasurable? For one reason: it causes those who have not yet attained faith to achieve perfect faith, gathering them back into a single thought-moment.

First, seeking outwardly; second, assisting those who have already developed faith to strengthen their power of contemplation, so that their principles and practice become firm and they may swiftly realize Bodhi—like riding a vast carriage to reach a treasury of jewels, or like boarding a sturdy ship to ascend the shore of enlightenment.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: The Buddha told Ānanda, "If there were someone who [filled] all the voids throughout the ten directions..."

"Suppose there were a space as vast as empty void, filled to the brim with the seven treasures, which one were to offer and present to as many Buddhas as there are motes of dust, serving and making offerings to them with a heart that never fails.
What do you think, Ānanda? By virtue of this cause and condition of giving to the Buddhas, would that person obtain much merit?
Ānanda replied, "The void is inexhaustible and precious jewels are boundless. Yet in the past, there was a sentient being who gave the Buddhas only seven coins, yet when he cast off his body..."
One would obtain the rank of a Wheel-Turning King; how much more so when [the merit] is manifested before one’s eyes?

Even if the entirety of space were filled with Buddha-fields and one bestowed precious jewels throughout them for an eon, even the most profound contemplation could not equal this merit—how, then, could it have any limit?
The Buddha told Ānanda: “The words of all Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are never false. If there should be a person who possesses the four grave offenses and the ten *pārājika* transgressions...”
In an instant, one passes through this world and other worlds, even unto the Avīci Hell, traversing all the uninterrupted realms throughout the ten directions without exception.
If one can, with a single thought, take up this Dharma-gate and reveal it to those who have not yet studied during the final kalpa,
that person’s karmic obstructions will be extinguished at that very moment, and the causes for the suffering of hell they were to undergo will be transformed into peace and happiness.

A person who attains this merit surpasses those who give material gifts by a hundredfold, a thousandfold, ten million billionfold, and even to the extent that it cannot be reached by calculation or analogy.
To praise the propagation of this scripture brings boundless benefit and excellence. The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* states:
"There are five superior benefits for one who gives the gift of Dharma. What are these five? First, the gift of Dharma provides benefit to both [self and others]."

The gift of material wealth is not like this. Second, the gift of Dharma can cause sentient beings to transcend the triple world, whereas the merit of the gift of material wealth does not transcend the desire realm.
Third, the gift of Dharma can purify the Dharma-body, whereas the gift of material wealth only increases physical form.
Fourth, the gift of Dharma is inexhaustible, whereas the gift of material wealth is exhaustible. Fifth, the gift of Dharma can sever ignorance, whereas the gift of material wealth only...

One subdues craving and attachment; therefore, son of good family, his merit is immeasurable and boundless, difficult to illustrate by analogy. Furthermore, the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states:
"The gift of the seven treasures throughout a trichiliocosm is not equal to receiving, upholding, and reciting even a four-line verse [of this sutra], or explaining it to others;
the latter brings forth greater merit than the former. If there are sons or daughters of good family who carve, print, and distribute [this scripture] for circulation...

It is transmitted that all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm shall suddenly awaken to the Supreme Vehicle of the One Vehicle, ascend together to the realm of the Buddhas, and collectively realize Bodhi.
Their merit is boundless and difficult to describe.

The single mind is the general characteristic of the myriad dharmas; the myriad dharmas are the particular characteristics of the single mind. There are two kinds of mind:
the true and the deluded, which differ from one another. By relying on the true mind, one swiftly realizes Bodhi; by following the deluded mind, one drifts through birth and death.

The true mind and the deluded mind both know that they are the fundamental substance. The true mind is spiritual awareness; it knows without knowing. The deluded mind is cognitive consciousness; it knows by means of knowing.
Knowing without knowing is perfectly luminous, quiescent, and illuminating. Knowing by means of knowing arises and perishes from moment to moment.
